facts: The robin tilts its head sideways, listening. Or watching. Hard to say which, with a robin.
First bird most people learn. Red breast, brown back, hopping along the lawn like it owns the place. It does, in a way.
Named for the European robin because of the orange chest. The two birds aren't related at all. People do this with names sometimes.
aldo.size: About the size of a softball, with a tail.
aldo.look: Brown above, rust-orange across the chest. The throat is streaked with white. Yellow bill, dark eye with a thin white ring. Hops, then stops, then hops.
aldo.home: Lawns and gardens, parks and forest edges. Anywhere there's short grass and worms underneath.

facts: The male is the brightest red thing in winter. Against snow, it looks almost too red to be allowed.
Both sexes sing, which is unusual. The female often sings from the nest.
Sometimes called the redbird. The crest goes up when something interests him.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow that has decided to be larger.
aldo.look: Male is all red with a black mask around the bill. The female is warm tan with red trim and the same crest. Both have a stout orange-red bill.
aldo.home: Yards and woodland edges, shrubs and gardens. They like a tangle to disappear into.

facts: A jay can sound like a hawk when it wants to. It clears the feeder this way. I have watched.
Mostly blue, but also white and black. The pattern on the wings is small and exact.
Lives in the same forests and yards all year, in most of its range. Some western birds migrate. Most don't bother.
aldo.size: A little smaller than a crow. Bigger than you remember.
aldo.look: Bright blue back and wings, a black necklace, white chest. The crest rises and falls with mood. The bill is sturdy.
aldo.home: Deciduous and pine woods, parks, backyards. Anywhere with acorns is a good guess.

facts: Crows know each other. They know us, too. There's a crow on my pond who watches me read.
All black. Not iridescent like a starling, not brown like a raven. Just black, with intelligence behind the eye.
Their call and the raven's call are different, even though the birds look alike. The crow says caw. The raven says something rougher.
aldo.size: About the size of a small house cat folded into wings.
aldo.look: Solid black, beak to feet. Stocky body, square tail, strong bill. They walk with a certain swagger.
aldo.home: Everywhere. Towns, fields, woods, beaches. Crows don't have a habitat so much as they have opinions.

facts: Their wings whistle when they take off. Not a song. A small mechanical hush.
One of the most numerous birds in North America. Twenty million of them, give or take, depending on the year.
Sometimes called the rain dove. The call sounds like sadness if you're in that mood, and like nothing if you aren't.
aldo.size: About the size of a long, soft sandwich.
aldo.look: Soft gray-brown all over. Long tapered tail with white edges. Small head, dark eye, thin black bill. A few black spots on the wing.
aldo.home: Open ground. Yards, farms, roadsides, parks. They like to perch on wires.

facts: Brought here from Europe in the 1800s. Now they live in cities all over the world. They came with us.
Males have a black bib and a gray cap. Females and young birds are pale brown all over.
About six inches long, around an ounce. Small, but they take up space at a feeder.
aldo.size: About the size of a small lemon.
aldo.look: Stout little bird, brown and gray. Males have a black throat and chest patch and a chestnut nape. Females are plainer, with a soft eyebrow stripe.
aldo.home: Wherever people are. Sidewalks, hedges, gas stations, eaves. They prefer the city to the woods.

facts: Iridescent black, all of them at once, when the light is right. In dull light they're just dark.
Fall and winter, the feathers have white spots like a starry sky. The spots wear off by spring.
Introduced from Europe in the 1890s. They got here, and stayed.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin, but stockier.
aldo.look: Glossy black with green and purple sheen. Yellow bill in breeding season, dark in winter. Short tail, pointed wings, walks rather than hops.
aldo.home: Cities, farms, fields, parking lots. They like open ground and a place to roost together at night.

facts: The black neck and the white chinstrap make it look like the goose is wearing a uniform.
Mostly grass and grain. A goose grazes like a small flat-footed cow.
They migrate, mostly. But some stay all year now, especially near parks and golf courses.
aldo.size: About the size of a basketball with a long neck.
aldo.look: Brown body, pale belly, black neck and head with a white patch on the cheek and chin. Black bill, black feet. They walk in a deliberate line.
aldo.home: Lakes, ponds, parks, fields, fairways. Anywhere flat with grass and water nearby.

facts: The drake's head looks green or purple depending on the light. Same feather, different angle.
Female is brown all over, mottled. Easier to lose against the cattails. That's the point.
Dabbling duck — tips forward, tail in the air, head underwater. Not a diver.
aldo.size: About the size of a small loaf of bread.
aldo.look: Drake has a glossy green head, white neck ring, chestnut chest, gray body, curled black tail feathers. Hen is mottled brown, with an orange bill blotched in black.
aldo.home: Ponds, marshes, lakes, slow rivers. Park ponds especially. They are comfortable around people.

facts: The tail is rusty red, but only on top, and only on adults. From below, you have to wait for it to bank.
Most common large hawk in North America. The one you see on a fencepost when you're driving somewhere.
The screams in movies, the ones a bald eagle is supposed to make — those are usually a red-tail. Eagles don't sound like that.
aldo.size: About the size of a small chicken with broader wings.
aldo.look: Brown above, pale below with a streaky belly band. Broad rounded wings. The red tail flashes when it banks. Yellow legs and feet.
aldo.home: Open country, roadsides, fields with a few trees. They like a high perch and a long view.

facts: Smallest woodpecker in North America. About the size of a sparrow with a chisel for a face.
Black and white all over, in tidy patterns. Males have a small red patch on the back of the head.
They tap. They tap, then they listen, then they tap again. Patient work.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow, more or less.
aldo.look: White below, black above with white spots on the wings. White stripe down the back. Short stubby bill. Male has a red dot on the back of the head.
aldo.home: Forests, yards with trees, parks. Anywhere there's bark to inspect.

facts: A bright yellow male in summer, and a dull olive bird in winter. Same bird, two seasons.
Migrates. Some go south, some shuffle just far enough to find food. They cross the Canadian border one way or the other.
Eats seeds, almost only seeds. A finch's whole life is a seed.
aldo.size: About the size of a small lemon, but thinner.
aldo.look: Summer male: bright yellow body, black cap and wings, white wing bars. Female and winter male: olive-brown, paler below, with the same wing bars. Short notched tail.
aldo.home: Weedy fields, garden edges, thistle patches, backyards with feeders.

facts: The song changes a little from one valley to the next. They learn from their neighbors.
Streaky brown breast with a dark central spot, like someone dropped one extra dot on purpose.
One of the most common sparrows in North America. Easy to overlook. Worth not overlooking.
aldo.size: About the size of a small egg with feathers.
aldo.look: Streaky brown above, white below with heavy brown streaks and a dark central breast spot. Long rounded tail. Pumps the tail in flight.
aldo.home: Shrubby places near water. Wetland edges, brambles, garden corners.

facts: On a cold night, they let their body temperature drop on purpose, to save energy. Wake up cold, warm up by morning.
Their memory for hidden seeds is better than yours. They cache thousands and find them again.
Says its own name, more or less. Chick-a-dee-dee-dee. The number of dees tells the others how worried to be.
aldo.size: About the size of a ping-pong ball with a tail.
aldo.look: Tiny round bird. Black cap, black throat, white cheeks, soft gray back, buff sides. Tiny dark bill. Always seems busy.
aldo.home: Mixed and deciduous forests, yards, parks. Anywhere with trees and a feeder helps.

facts: Loud for its size. A whole song coming out of a bird that fits in your hand.
Stays on its territory all year. Pairs stay together. They sing to each other through the winter.
Cold winters push them back south. Warm winters let them creep northward again. They follow weather, slowly.
aldo.size: About the size of a small plum.
aldo.look: Warm rusty brown above, buff below. Bold white eyebrow stripe. Long curved bill. Tail held up at an angle, often.
aldo.home: Brushy yards, woodland edges, tangles. They like a porch to nest on, or an old boot.

facts: Male sings from the top of a cattail, red shoulder flashed forward. The whole marsh is divided up this way.
Female looks like a giant streaky sparrow. Easy to miss her in the reeds.
Red shoulder patch with a yellow border. He flashes it on purpose. Most of the time it's hidden.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin.
aldo.look: Male is glossy black with a red shoulder patch edged in yellow. Female is brown, heavily streaked, with a pale eyebrow. Pointed bill. Slightly notched tail.
aldo.home: Marshes, wet fields, ditches with cattails. They show up in dry fields too, in winter flocks.

facts: Small gray bird with big dark eyes. They stare back at you longer than most birds do.
The crest gives it away. Without the crest it would be a forgettable gray bird.
South Texas has a separate species, the black-crested titmouse. Same kind of bird, different cap.
aldo.size: About the size of a chickadee with better posture.
aldo.look: Soft gray above, white below, peach-colored flanks. Pointed gray crest. Big dark eyes set in a pale face.
aldo.home: Deciduous forests and shady yards. They like oaks especially.

facts: Walks down the tree headfirst. Most birds go up. The nuthatch sees the bark from a different angle.
Pale blue-gray back, white face and belly, black cap, chestnut under the tail. Stocky and short-tailed.
Strong feet and a thick bill. Built for prying things out of bark.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow, but rounder.
aldo.look: Stocky bird. Pale blue-gray above, clean white below and on the face. Black cap on males, dark gray on females. Sharp pointed bill.
aldo.home: Mature woods, parks, yards with big trees. They like oaks and beeches.

facts: The scientific name means many-tongued mimic. It earns the name. A mockingbird can imitate dozens of other birds, and a car alarm.
Mostly stays put. Northern birds may shift south in hard winters.
Slim, gray, long tail. White flashes on the wings when it flies.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin, but slimmer.
aldo.look: Gray above, paler below. Two white wing bars and a big white wing patch that flashes in flight. Long tail with white outer feathers. Yellow eye.
aldo.home: Yards, hedgerows, parking lots, scrubby edges. Anywhere with a high perch to sing from.

facts: Sometimes called the snowbird. Shows up in yards when it gets cold, and disappears in spring.
Dark hood, white belly, pink bill. The pattern is plain on purpose.
When they fly off, the white outer tail feathers flash. That's how you know.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow.
aldo.look: Slate gray above and across the chest, white belly. Pink-ivory bill. White outer tail feathers visible in flight. Western birds have brown backs and rusty sides.
aldo.home: Forests in summer, yards and feeders in winter. Likes the ground under a hedge.

facts: The blue is so pure on a male in spring it almost doesn't look like an animal color.
State bird of Missouri and New York. Twice honored.
Likes a fence post or low branch, hunting bugs by dropping down to grab them.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow.
aldo.look: Male: bright blue head, back, and wings; rusty orange chest; white belly. Female is paler, gray-blue with a softer orange wash. Stout small bill.
aldo.home: Open fields, meadows, orchards, golf course edges. They nest in cavities and boxes.

facts: Originally a western bird. Released in New York in the 1940s, and now they're everywhere.
Males vary in color. Bright red is the standard, but some are orange, and a few are yellow. The food they eat tints the feathers.
Females are streaky brown, plain. They're the same shape as the male but without the paint.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow.
aldo.look: Male has red on the head, throat, and chest, with a brown streaky back and belly. Female is brown all over with blurry streaks. Stout, slightly curved bill.
aldo.home: Cities, suburbs, yards. They like buildings and feeders. Less common in deep woods.

facts: Spends winter in Central America and Mexico. Crosses the Gulf of Mexico in one go, both ways. Three grams of bird, six hundred miles of water.
Most common hummingbird east of the Mississippi. The only one most people will see in that half of the country.
Male's throat looks black until the light catches it. Then it's a red so bright it almost hums.
aldo.size: About the size of your thumb.
aldo.look: Tiny. Iridescent green back, white belly. Male has a ruby-red gorget on the throat that flashes in light. Female has a clean white throat. Long needle bill.
aldo.home: Gardens, forest edges, anywhere with tube-shaped flowers. Sugar-water feeders too.

facts: I have been startled by a heron exactly twice. They're quiet until they aren't.
Stands very still in shallow water. Then strikes. The whole point of a heron is patience.
Common all over North America near water. Caribbean and Florida have an all-white form.
aldo.size: About the size of a fourth-grader, mostly legs and neck.
aldo.look: Tall blue-gray bird. Long neck, long yellow legs, long pointed bill. Black plumes off the back of the head. Flies with the neck folded back.
aldo.home: Wetlands, pond edges, tidal flats, river shallows. Anywhere a fish might be.

facts: The red bald head is so it can stick its face into things and not get its feathers messy.
Soars with the wings held in a shallow V. From a long way off, that's how you tell it's a vulture and not a hawk.
Smells carrion from miles away. Most birds can't smell much. The turkey vulture is an exception.
aldo.size: About the size of a small turkey, hence the name.
aldo.look: Big dark bird with a long, broad-winged silhouette. Wings held in a V when soaring. Bare red head on adults, gray on young birds. Two-toned underwing.
aldo.home: Open country, roadsides, deserts, forests, suburbs. They go where the dead are.

facts: Deeply forked tail. The point of the fork is what catches the eye when one zips past.
Builds a mud nest under barn eaves and bridges. They like to be over your head.
Almost always seen flying. They feed on the wing, eating insects out of the air.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow with longer everything.
aldo.look: Steel-blue back, rusty throat, buff or rusty belly. Long forked tail with white spots. Pointed wings. Quick acrobatic flight.
aldo.home: Open fields, farms, ponds, near barns and bridges. They like a roof to nest under.

facts: The red is mostly on the head, not the belly. The belly red is faint, and you almost never see it.
Zebra back. Black and white bars all the way down.
Common in eastern yards and woods. They visit feeders for suet.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin.
aldo.look: Pale gray underneath with a faint reddish wash on the belly. Bold black-and-white barred back. Bright red cap and nape on the male. Female has red only on the nape.
aldo.home: Eastern forests, yards, parks. They like big deciduous trees.

facts: Built for chasing other birds through the woods. Long tail to steer, short rounded wings to dodge.
Easy to mix up with the smaller sharp-shinned hawk. Same shape, different size, different proportions.
Female is bigger than the male, like most birds of prey. The bigger one does the bigger work.
aldo.size: About the size of a crow with longer legs.
aldo.look: Slate-gray back, rust-barred chest, long banded tail with a rounded tip. Red eye in adults, yellow in young birds. Yellow legs.
aldo.home: Forests and forest edges, increasingly suburbs and yards. Wherever bird feeders bring small birds.

facts: Bigger than you remember. A male with his tail fanned takes up half a clearing.
Iridescent feathers — bronze, copper, green — that look almost gray from a distance.
Can fly, surprisingly well, in short bursts. Roosts in trees at night.
aldo.size: About the size of a folded card table, mostly feathers.
aldo.look: Large ground bird. Dark iridescent body, bare bluish-red head, fan tail when displaying. Males have a beard of bristles on the chest. Strong legs.
aldo.home: Woods, edges, fields. They walk in groups along tree lines.

facts: Smallest falcon in North America. Bright as a parrot up close, plain at a distance.
Hovers over fields. Quick wingbeats, head perfectly still, watching the grass below.
Two black slashes down the face. Like it's wearing the same eyeliner twice.
aldo.size: About the size of a mourning dove.
aldo.look: Small falcon. Male has a slate-blue head and wings, rusty back and tail. Female is rusty and barred all over. Two vertical black face stripes. Long tail, pointed wings.
aldo.home: Open fields, roadsides, fence wires, telephone poles. Anywhere with a high perch and grass below.

facts: Sometimes called the fish hawk. Sometimes river hawk, sea hawk. The osprey eats fish almost only.
Two feet long, six feet across the wings. Big for a hawk. Bigger than you expect.
Brown back, white head and chest, dark eye stripe. Almost everywhere there's water and a tall pole to nest on.
aldo.size: About the size of a hawk wearing eagle's wings.
aldo.look: Brown above, white below with a clean white head and a dark eye stripe. Long crooked wings. The toes have spines for gripping fish.
aldo.home: Coasts, lakes, rivers. Anywhere there are fish near the surface and somewhere tall to nest.

facts: Sometimes called the tiger of the air. Eats rabbits and mice and skunks and other birds. Almost anything it can catch.
The most widespread true owl in the Americas. Deserts, forests, swamps, cities — they make do.
The horns aren't horns. They're tufts of feathers. They look serious, but they don't do anything.
aldo.size: About the size of a housecat with feathers on top.
aldo.look: Big stocky owl. Mottled gray-brown body, white throat, large yellow eyes, ear tufts. The face is round and cupped, like a satellite dish for sound.
aldo.home: Almost everywhere. Forests, parks, deserts, edges of towns. Where there is night and prey, there is a great horned owl.

facts: Lives near water with old-growth trees. Big enough to need a big tree.
The white head and tail come in around five years old. Younger birds are mottled brown all over and easy to mistake for something else.
Whole continent of America, from Alaska down through Mexico. They went away for a while. They came back.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog with a six-foot wingspan.
aldo.look: Adult: dark brown body, bright white head and tail, big yellow bill, yellow eyes and feet. Juvenile: dark brown all over with white speckling. Heavy, broad wings.
aldo.home: Lakes, rivers, coasts. Where the fish are. They like a tall, sturdy tree for the nest.

facts: Most owls have yellow eyes. The barred owl has dark brown ones. That's part of why the face looks soft.
Lives in the swamps and old woods of the eastern half of the country.
Round face, no ear tufts, gray-brown all over with vertical streaks below.
aldo.size: About the size of a small bowling pin in a feather coat.
aldo.look: Stocky brown owl with a round face, no ear tufts, dark eyes. Brown bars across the chest, vertical streaks down the belly.
aldo.home: Mature woods, especially wet ones. River bottoms, cypress swamps, old hardwoods.

facts: Named for the wax-like red drops at the wingtips. They look painted on, but they're feathers.
Eats berries. Whole berries, all winter. Sometimes a flock will pass berries down a branch, beak to beak.
Travels in groups. You hear the high thin call before you see them.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin, but slimmer.
aldo.look: Sleek brown body, pale yellow belly, gray wings, black mask edged in white. Yellow band at the tail tip. Crested head.
aldo.home: Open woods and edges, suburbs, anywhere with berry trees. Cedars, hollies, crabapples.

facts: The kingfisher rattles when it flies. The call sounds like a tiny outboard motor.
Female has more color than the male, which is unusual. She has a rusty band across the belly. He doesn't.
Hovers over water, drops, comes up with a fish. Then back to a branch to eat it head-first.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin, but with a bigger head.
aldo.look: Stocky blue-gray bird with a shaggy crest, big bill, white collar, blue chest band. Female adds a rusty belly band. Short legs, big head.
aldo.home: Streams, ponds, coasts, slow rivers. Anywhere with clear water and a perch over it.

facts: Two black bands across the chest. Most plovers have one. Killdeer have two, and that's how you know.
Named for its call. It says its own name, kill-deer kill-deer, over and over.
When something gets near the nest, the parent fakes a broken wing and limps away. Leads you off, then suddenly flies up fine.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin.
aldo.look: Brown back with reddish edges, white belly, two black breast bands. Long legs, slender body, big dark eye. Rusty rump shows in flight.
aldo.home: Open ground. Gravel parking lots, fields, riverbanks, rooftops. Not just shorelines.

facts: Bright yellow chest with a black V. From the back, brown and streaky. From the front, you can't miss it.
Eastern and western meadowlarks look almost identical. Their songs are different. That's how birds tell them apart.
Sings from a fence post or a tall weed. The song carries across grass for a long way.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin.
aldo.look: Stocky brown bird, streaked above, with a bright yellow throat and chest crossed by a sharp black V. White outer tail feathers in flight.
aldo.home: Grasslands, prairies, hayfields, pastures. Open country with tall grass.

facts: Crow-sized. Second-biggest woodpecker in the country, after the ivory-billed, which is probably gone.
The red crest gives the bird its name. Pileatus is Latin for capped.
Carves rectangular holes in dead trees. Big ones. You can spot the work before you spot the bird.
aldo.size: About the size of a crow with a tall red hat.
aldo.look: Big black woodpecker with a flaming red crest, white stripe on the face and neck, white wing patches in flight. Heavy chisel bill.
aldo.home: Mature forests, eastern and Pacific Northwest. They need big old trees.

facts: The male is the orange and black of Lord Baltimore's coat of arms. That's how the bird got its name.
Hangs a sock-shaped nest out at the end of a branch. Mostly elm and other tall hardwoods.
Spends winter in Central America. Comes back to eastern yards for the summer.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin.
aldo.look: Male: black head and back, bright orange chest and belly, black-and-white wings. Female: olive-yellow with grayer wings. Long pointed bill.
aldo.home: Tall deciduous trees, edges, parks, yards with shade trees. They like an open canopy.

facts: The blue isn't pigment. It's the way the feather scatters light. In shade the bird looks black.
Male is electric blue all over in summer. Female is plain warm brown. Both have a stout finch bill.
Sings from a high perch all day. Pairs of paired notes, over and over.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow.
aldo.look: Small finch-like bird. Breeding male is bright blue all over, deepest on the head. Female and winter male: warm brown, paler below, with a hint of blue in the wings.
aldo.home: Brushy edges, old fields, roadsides with weeds. They like an opening with songposts.

facts: Most colorful duck on the continent. The drake looks like he was painted by someone showing off.
Sometimes called the Carolina duck. Lives in wooded swamps and pond edges.
Nests in tree cavities. The ducklings jump out the morning after they hatch — sometimes from forty feet up.
aldo.size: About the size of a small football.
aldo.look: Drake: green crested head with white stripes, chestnut chest with white spots, buff sides, dark back. Hen: gray-brown with a white teardrop around the eye, soft crest.
aldo.home: Wooded swamps, beaver ponds, slow streams with overhanging trees.

facts: Black ring around a yellow bill. That's the field mark. The rest is gull.
Common all over the country, including parking lots and dumpster lids. Not picky.
Named for the Delaware River, where the bird was first described.
aldo.size: About the size of a small duck, but standing on long legs.
aldo.look: Medium gull. Pale gray back, white head and underparts, yellow bill with a black ring near the tip, yellow legs. Black wingtips with white spots.
aldo.home: Lakes, beaches, parks, parking lots, fields. Anywhere with food and open space.

facts: Dives for fish from the air. Wings folded, hits the water like a thrown blanket.
One of two pelican species in the Americas that fishes by diving. The other is the Peruvian pelican.
The pouch holds gallons. Not for storage — for scooping. The water drains out, the fish stays.
aldo.size: About the size of a four-year-old, mostly bill.
aldo.look: Big gray-brown bird with a long bill, large throat pouch, broad wings. Adults have white heads with a yellow wash, dark bodies. Young birds are duller and browner.
aldo.home: Coasts. Atlantic, Gulf, Pacific. Piers, jetties, sandbars. They roost in groups.

facts: On the Platte River in Nebraska, hundreds of thousands of cranes stop over every spring. Half a million wings, more or less, all in one stretch of river.
Tall gray bird with a red patch on the forehead. Long neck out straight in flight, not folded back like a heron.
Their call carries for miles. A rolling sound that doesn't sound like a bird at first.
aldo.size: About the size of a child, on stilts.
aldo.look: Tall gray bird with a red crown patch, long neck, long legs. Sometimes stained rusty from preening with iron-rich mud. Bushy tertial feathers droop over the tail.
aldo.home: Wetlands, fields, river sandbars. Open country with shallow water nearby.

facts: Stays west all year. Most hummingbirds migrate. Anna's tough it out.
Male's gorget is rose-red, but only when the light catches it right. Otherwise dark.
Common in West Coast gardens and chaparral. Will visit a feeder in winter without fuss.
aldo.size: About the size of your thumb.
aldo.look: Small green-backed hummingbird. Male has a rose-red crown and throat that flash in the right light. Female: green back, gray throat with a few red spots, white-tipped tail.
aldo.home: Gardens, chaparral, parks, suburbs along the West Coast.

facts: The blue jay's western cousin. Same shape, same crest. Black head and chest instead of blue and white.
Only crested jay west of the Rockies.
Lives in mountain forests and campgrounds. Quick to claim a picnic table.
aldo.size: About the size of a small crow.
aldo.look: Dark blue body, deep blue wings and tail with fine black bars, sooty black head and chest, tall pointed crest.
aldo.home: Mountain conifer forests, mixed woods. Campgrounds, lodges, anywhere people leave food.

facts: Sky blue all over. Not the blue and orange of the eastern bluebird. Just blue.
Western bird. Mountain meadows, sagebrush, open country with scattered trees.
Hovers when hunting bugs in tall grass. Most bluebirds drop from a perch. This one floats.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow.
aldo.look: Slim thrush. Male: sky-blue all over, paler below. Female: gray-brown body with blue tinges in the wings and tail.
aldo.home: Mountain meadows, sagebrush, open grasslands with scattered trees and nest cavities.

facts: Yellow body, black wings, red face on the male. Looks tropical, but it nests up in the conifers.
Used to be in the tanager family. Now classified with the cardinals.
Female is plainer — yellow-green with darker wings. Easy to overlook against pine needles.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow.
aldo.look: Stocky songbird. Male: yellow body, black wings with a yellow shoulder bar, red-orange wash on the face. Female: yellowish-green with grayer wings.
aldo.home: Conifer and mixed forests in the western mountains, especially in summer.

facts: The male looks like a small color wheel. Red below, blue head, green back. Nothing else looks like it.
First-year males look like females — yellow-green. They get the colors in their second year.
Brushy edges in the southeast and parts of Texas. They sneak in and out of the tangles.
aldo.size: About the size of a sparrow.
aldo.look: Male: blue head, lime-green back, bright red underparts and rump. Female and first-year male: lime-green and yellow-green, paler below. Stout finch bill.
aldo.home: Brushy fields, woodland edges, weedy roadsides in the Southeast and southern Plains.

facts: Hunts in daylight. Most owls don't. The snowy lives where there's no real night for half the year.
Males are almost pure white. Females have black flecks. Young birds are flecked all over.
Nests on the Arctic ground, not in trees. Comes south in winter, mostly to open country and beach dunes.
aldo.size: About the size of a small grocery bag, full.
aldo.look: Big white owl. Round head, no ear tufts, yellow eyes, feathered legs and feet. Heavy body, broad wings.
aldo.home: Open country in winter — fields, dunes, airports, lakeshores. Arctic tundra in summer.

facts: Pink, with a spoon for a bill. Sweeps it side to side through shallow water, snapping up shrimp.
The pink comes from what they eat. Like flamingos.
Florida and the Gulf Coast. Mangroves and shallow coastal water.
aldo.size: About the size of a great blue heron, but pinker.
aldo.look: Tall pink wading bird with a long flat spoon-tipped bill. Bald greenish head on adults. Pink wings, brighter at the shoulder, and red legs.
aldo.home: Coastal wetlands, mangroves, salt flats, shallow estuaries.

facts: Fastest animal on Earth in a dive. Two hundred miles an hour, give or take, when it's stooping on prey.
Sometimes called the duck hawk. Eats other birds, mostly, taken in the air.
Female is larger than the male. The male is called a tiercel — meaning a third smaller.
aldo.size: About the size of a crow with sharper edges.
aldo.look: Slate blue-gray back, white chest with fine dark bars, black hood and mustache stripe. Pointed wings, long tapered tail.
aldo.home: Cliffs, bridges, tall buildings. Cities suit them now. They like a high ledge over open space.

facts: Looks bigger than it is. Most of the size is feathers. The bird underneath is smaller than a great horned.
Round gray face, yellow eyes, no ear tufts. The face has rings, like a target.
Hunts by ear. Can hear a vole moving under a foot of snow.
aldo.size: About the size of a basketball, in feathers.
aldo.look: Tall gray owl. Big round face with concentric gray rings, yellow eyes, white bow-tie under the bill. Heavy gray-brown body with fine streaks.
aldo.home: Boreal and montane forests, often near meadow edges. Northern Rockies and the upper Great Lakes.

facts: Tallest bird in North America. Five feet of crane.
Almost gone in the 1940s. Down to about twenty birds. Now several hundred, slowly. The work isn't done.
White all over with black wingtips, red crown patch, yellow eye. They live a long time — twenty years or more in the wild.
aldo.size: About the size of a kindergartener with longer legs.
aldo.look: Tall white crane with black wingtips visible only in flight, red bare-skin crown, dark mustache, long legs and neck. Long pointed bill.
aldo.home: Coastal marshes in winter (Texas), shallow wetlands and prairie pools in summer (reintroduced flock in Wisconsin).

facts: Biggest land bird in North America. Wingspan close to nine feet.
Was extinct in the wild in 1987. Every wild bird was caught and bred in zoos. Then put back, slowly. Some are flying again now.
Bald head, like a vulture's. The skin changes color when the bird is excited.
aldo.size: About the size of a small child with enormous wings.
aldo.look: Massive black bird with a bare orange-pink head, white triangle on the underwing, dark body. Numbered tags on the wing in the wild — every bird is known.
aldo.home: Canyons, mountains, cliffs of California, Arizona, Utah. Reintroduced range only.

facts: The tail is twice as long as the bird. Forks deep, opens and closes like scissors when it flies.
Perches on fence wires in the southern plains, then sallies after insects.
Pale gray body, salmon-pink underwings and flanks. The tail is the giveaway from a long way off.
aldo.size: About the size of a robin, with the tail trailing far behind.
aldo.look: Slender pale-gray bird with a long deeply forked tail, salmon-pink wash on the flanks and underwing. Dark wings, white outer tail feathers.
aldo.home: Open prairies, fences, scattered trees in the southern plains.

facts: A cuckoo that runs instead of flies, mostly. Can fly, but doesn't bother for short trips.
Sometimes called snake killer. Catches lizards, snakes, scorpions. The desert is full of food if you can grab it.
Streaky brown body, shaggy crest, long tail. They run with the head out and the tail trailing.
aldo.size: About the size of a small chicken.
aldo.look: Long-legged ground bird. Streaky brown above, pale buff below, shaggy dark crest, blue and red bare skin behind the eye. Long tail held flat behind.
aldo.home: Deserts, scrub, mesquite flats, open areas with low cover.

facts: Their call is the call of the north woods. A long wail, then a yodel. Carries across a still lake.
Swims underwater chasing fish. The eye is red — that part is just true.
Black and white checkerboard back in summer. In winter they go gray and dull and move to the coast.
aldo.size: About the size of a small goose with a sharp beak.
aldo.look: Large black-and-white diving bird. Breeding adult: black head with greenish gloss, dagger bill, white-and-black checkered back, white belly, red eye. Non-breeding: dull gray-brown above, white below.
aldo.home: Clear northern lakes in summer. Coasts and large bays in winter.

facts: The orange and yellow on the bill come and go with the season. Bright in summer, dull in winter. The face does a costume change.
Only Atlantic puffin in the Atlantic. The other puffins live on the Pacific side.
Nests in burrows on rocky islands. In Maine, only on a few islands offshore.
aldo.size: About the size of a small football.
aldo.look: Stout black-and-white seabird. Black back and crown, white face and belly, orange feet, broad triangular bill striped orange, yellow, and gray in summer.
aldo.home: Rocky coastal islands in summer for nesting. Open ocean the rest of the year.

facts: A squirrel buries an acorn and forgets where most of them are. The forgotten ones become trees. The squirrel plants forests by accident.
Native to the eastern half of the country. Introduced to England, where it caused trouble for the red squirrel that was already there.
Gray on the back, white below, big bushy tail held over the shoulder. Some are all-black instead — same species, different paint.
aldo.size: About the size of a loaf of bread, half of which is tail.
aldo.look: Tree squirrel with gray-brown fur, paler underside, big plumed tail. Bright dark eye. Holds food in front paws. Some populations are entirely black.
aldo.home: Yards with oak trees, parks, deciduous forests. They follow nuts.

facts: When a deer runs, the tail goes up. White underside, flagged like a flashlight back at the herd.
Most widely distributed wild hoofed animal in the Americas. From Canada down to Bolivia.
Bucks shed their antlers every year. New ones grow in covered in velvet — soft skin, full of blood vessels — until autumn.
aldo.size: About the size of a large dog, on stilts.
aldo.look: Reddish-brown in summer, gray-brown in winter. White belly and throat. White underside of the tail flashes when alarmed. Bucks have branched antlers; does don't.
aldo.home: Forest edges, suburbs, fields. They live wherever there's cover and a salad nearby.

facts: Sits very still until you're almost on top of it, then bolts. The cotton ball tail flashes white as it goes.
One of the most common rabbits in North America.
Eats grass and clover in summer. Bark and twigs in winter. They make do.
aldo.size: About the size of a small loaf of bread.
aldo.look: Soft brown rabbit with a white belly, white tail underneath, long ears, dark eye. Stays low to the ground. Front paws tucked under when at rest.
aldo.home: Yards, weedy fields, brushy edges, brambles. Anywhere with cover and grass.

facts: Hands more than paws. They feel things, often in water. The species name lotor means washer.
Black mask across the eyes, ringed tail, gray fur. The mask doesn't actually hide them but it's where the cartoon comes from.
Native to North America. They've moved into cities, garbage cans, attics, anywhere with a lid that can be opened.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog with very busy hands.
aldo.look: Stocky, gray-brown body, black mask edged in white, black-and-white ringed tail. Pointed muzzle, alert dark eyes, dexterous front paws.
aldo.home: Forests, wetlands, suburbs, cities. They prefer somewhere with water and a lot of food options.

facts: Largest tree squirrel in North America. Bigger than the gray. Slower, too.
Often orange-brown all over, but it varies. Some are silver, some are nearly black, some have white faces. Same species.
Likes oak savannas and open parks more than dense woods.
aldo.size: About the size of a small house cat with a fluffier tail.
aldo.look: Big tree squirrel with a heavy build, rusty orange to gray-brown fur, paler belly, bushy tail. Long whiskers, dark eye.
aldo.home: Open oak forests, pecan groves, parks, suburbs. They like a few big trees with space between them.

facts: Stripes down the back. Dark, light, dark, light, dark. Five stripes, neat as paint.
The name comes from an Ojibwe word that means one who descends trees headlong. Which is exactly how they come down.
Cheek pouches stretch enormously. Stuffs them with seeds, runs home, empties them, runs back.
aldo.size: About the size of a small banana.
aldo.look: Small striped ground squirrel. Reddish-brown back with dark and light stripes from neck to tail. White belly. Big bright eye, twitchy little tail.
aldo.home: Deciduous forests, rocky areas, stone walls, yards with cover. They like a hole near a log.

facts: The only marsupial north of Mexico. Their babies grow up in a pouch, like a kangaroo's.
Plays dead when really threatened. Goes stiff, drools, slows the breathing. Not a trick — the body just does it.
Cat-sized, gray, hairless tail, pointed snout. Lots of small sharp teeth. They smile a lot, by accident.
aldo.size: About the size of a housecat with a rat tail.
aldo.look: Stocky gray-white animal with a pointed pink snout, naked ears, long pink prehensile tail. Black eyes, long whiskers, fifty teeth.
aldo.home: Woods, suburbs, garages, attics, alleys. They go where the food is and they eat almost anything.

facts: The smell carries half a mile in still air. Hard to forget.
Black with two white stripes that fork at the shoulders, meet at the head.
They warn you first. Stamp the front feet, raise the tail, sometimes do a little handstand. If you're still there, that's your problem.
aldo.size: About the size of a housecat with a feather duster.
aldo.look: Stocky black mammal with a white stripe down the forehead and a V on the back that splits into two long white stripes. Bushy black-and-white tail.
aldo.home: Woodland edges, fields, suburbs, farms. They like cover near food.

facts: Sometimes called a woodchuck. Doesn't chuck wood. The name is from an Algonquian word.
Hibernates through the winter. Their body slows almost to a stop. Wakes up in spring, comes out, eats clover.
Stands up on its hind legs to look around. Same shape as the prairie dog, but bigger and alone.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog, more square.
aldo.look: Chunky brown rodent with short legs, a short bushy tail, small rounded ears, dark eye. Stands upright at the burrow entrance to look around.
aldo.home: Field edges, meadows, embankments, roadside ditches, yards. They dig burrows in well-drained soil.

facts: Smaller than a wolf, larger than a fox. Looks like a thin dog with a long muzzle.
Lives in every continental state now. They followed people across the country and stayed.
Eats almost anything. Mice, rabbits, grasshoppers, fruit, garbage. Generalists do well.
aldo.size: About the size of a medium dog with a longer tail.
aldo.look: Slim canid with grizzled gray-brown fur, rusty legs and ears, black-tipped tail. Pointed muzzle, yellow eyes, alert ears.
aldo.home: Everywhere. Deserts, forests, prairies, suburbs, even cities.

facts: A red fox watched me once for a full minute. I was reading. Or pretending to read. He left first.
Largest of the true foxes. Also the most widespread carnivore on the planet — they're across most of the Northern Hemisphere.
Orange-red, white throat, black legs, white tail tip. The white tail tip is how you tell them apart from a coyote at distance.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog with a more important-looking tail.
aldo.look: Slender fox with rusty-orange fur, white chin, white belly, black socks, big ears. Long bushy tail with a white tip. Yellow-amber eyes.
aldo.home: Fields, forests, hedgerows, suburbs. They like edges between cover and open ground.

facts: Builds dams. Whole streams change because of beaver work. Ponds appear where there were rapids.
Largest rodent in North America after — actually, no, they're the largest. Up to sixty pounds.
Tail is flat, hairless, paddle-shaped. They slap it on water as a warning before diving.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog with a paddle for a tail.
aldo.look: Heavy-bodied rodent with thick brown fur, small ears, big orange front teeth, webbed back feet, broad scaly tail. Sits up on the haunches to chew.
aldo.home: Streams, rivers, ponds. Anywhere they can dam water and build a lodge of sticks and mud.

facts: Named for the ears. They're large, like a mule's. The ears keep moving even when the deer is still.
Western deer. Bigger and grayer than the white-tailed, with a black-tipped tail instead of a white flag.
When startled, they bounce on all four feet at once. Stiff-legged. Like they're on springs.
aldo.size: About the size of a large dog, with bigger ears than you'd guess.
aldo.look: Stocky gray-brown deer with a white rump, narrow black-tipped tail, large ears. Bucks have forked antlers that branch in pairs.
aldo.home: Mountain forests, deserts, sagebrush, rim country. Western half of the country.

facts: Mostly black, but not always. Can be cinnamon, chocolate, blonde, or even white in some places. Same species.
Smaller than a grizzly. No big shoulder hump. Round ears, short snout.
Climbs well. Almost any bear in a tree is a black bear, not a grizzly.
aldo.size: About the size of a folded-up couch.
aldo.look: Medium-sized bear with shaggy fur, usually black with a tan muzzle and sometimes a white chest patch. Round ears, no shoulder hump, straight face profile.
aldo.home: Forests of all kinds — deciduous, conifer, swamp, mountain. Where there are berries and acorns and quiet.

facts: Climbs trees. The only American canid that does, really. They sleep in branches sometimes.
Gray on the back, rusty on the sides, white below, black-tipped tail. Different from the red fox.
Lives across most of the country, but you see them less than red foxes. They prefer brushy cover and night.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog.
aldo.look: Salt-and-pepper gray back, rusty-orange sides and ears, white throat and chest. Long tail with a black ridge and black tip. Slim, low-slung body.
aldo.home: Forests, brushy edges, rocky places. They like cover and a tree to climb.

facts: Otters slide on snow and mud just to get places. Nothing else moves like that.
Thick, water-repellent fur. They float low in the water with the head and tail showing.
Up to thirty pounds, but built like a stretched weasel.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog with a long body.
aldo.look: Long sleek mammal with dense brown fur, paler throat and belly, webbed feet, thick tapering tail. Small ears, whiskered muzzle, dark bright eyes.
aldo.home: Rivers, lakes, marshes, coasts. Anywhere there's clean water and fish.

facts: About twice the size of a housecat. Most people never see one even where they're common.
Short black-tipped tail — the bob. That's the name.
Spotted, with black tufts on the ears and a ruff of fur on the cheeks.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog, in a fur coat that's too big.
aldo.look: Tan to gray-brown wild cat with dark spots and stripes, short bobbed tail with a black tip on top, tufted ears, side whiskers. Long legs.
aldo.home: Forests, swamps, deserts, brushy edges. Almost anywhere with cover and small prey.

facts: Shell made of bony plates with leathery skin between. Most of the body is armored, but the belly is soft.
Ancestors came up from South America when the Isthmus of Panama formed. They've been moving north ever since.
Always has four identical pups. Always. Same egg, split four ways.
aldo.size: About the size of a small housecat in armor.
aldo.look: Pinkish-gray armored mammal with bony plates banded across the back, scaly tail, long pointed snout, peg-like teeth, big ears. Strong digging claws.
aldo.home: Forests, brush, fields, yards across the southern US. They dig burrows.

facts: One of the largest deer in the world. Bulls in autumn weigh seven hundred pounds and carry antlers that branch six points or more.
Wapiti is a Shawnee word meaning white rump. The name fits — the rear is pale buff-cream.
Bulls bugle in the rut. A rising whistle that drops into a grunt. Carries miles in a mountain valley.
aldo.size: About the size of a small horse with antlers.
aldo.look: Large tan-bodied deer with a darker neck mane, pale rump and tail, long legs. Bulls have heavy branched antlers; cows do not.
aldo.home: Mountain meadows, forest edges, parks, river bottoms in the West. Some reintroduced herds in the East.

facts: Fastest land animal in the Americas. Built to outrun a cat that went extinct ten thousand years ago. Still running, just in case.
Sometimes called the American antelope. Not actually an antelope. Closest living relatives are giraffes.
Tan and white, with a black mask on the buck and twin horns that fork forward. They shed the outer sheath every year.
aldo.size: About the size of a medium dog with longer legs.
aldo.look: Slender hoofed animal with a tan back, white belly and rump, white throat patches. Bucks have black-and-white face markings and pronged horns. Big black eyes.
aldo.home: Open prairies, sagebrush flats, short-grass steppe. They want open country and a long view.

facts: Once tens of millions across the plains. Down to a few hundred by 1900. Now several hundred thousand again, in parks and refuges.
Sometimes called buffalo, though true buffalo live in Africa and Asia. The name stuck anyway.
Massive humped shoulders, shaggy head and front, smaller back end. They shed in spring and look terrible for a few weeks.
aldo.size: About the size of a small car.
aldo.look: Huge dark brown mammal with a high humped shoulder, shaggy head and forequarters, short black horns curving up and in, beard under the chin. Smaller hindquarters.
aldo.home: Prairies and grasslands, mostly in protected places now — Yellowstone, Wind Cave, the National Bison Range, a few others.

facts: Largest deer in the world. Bulls stand seven feet at the shoulder. Antlers spread six feet across.
The antlers are flat and palmate — wide and shovel-like. Other deer have antlers that branch like twigs.
Eats waterweed in summer. Wades into ponds, sticks the head under, comes up with a mouthful.
aldo.size: About the size of a horse with the wrong proportions.
aldo.look: Huge dark-brown deer with long legs, a humped shoulder, drooping nose, dewlap under the throat. Bulls have wide palmate antlers; cows do not.
aldo.home: Wetlands, boreal forest, willow thickets, lakes. They like cold and wet.

facts: Goes by many names. Mountain lion, cougar, puma, panther, catamount. The same cat, all the way from Yukon to Argentina.
Most widely distributed large cat in the western hemisphere. Adaptable. Lives almost anywhere with cover and deer.
Tan all over, long heavy tail nearly as long as the body, small round head. Adults don't have spots.
aldo.size: About the size of a large dog, but quieter.
aldo.look: Big tan cat with a paler belly, dark muzzle, long thick tail with a dark tip. Long muscular body, small rounded head, short ears.
aldo.home: Mountains, forests, desert canyons, swamp edges. Western US mostly, with a small population in southern Florida.

facts: They live in towns. Underground tunnels with hundreds of entrances, sentinels at each one.
Don't truly hibernate. You can see them above ground in midwinter on warm days.
A town in Texas once covered twenty-five thousand square miles. Hundreds of millions of prairie dogs in one connected city.
aldo.size: About the size of a fat cat squatting upright.
aldo.look: Stocky tan-brown rodent with a paler belly, short legs, short black-tipped tail, small ears, big dark eye. Sits upright at the burrow.
aldo.home: Short-grass and mixed-grass prairies of the Great Plains. Open country with packed soil for burrowing.

facts: Sometimes called the sea cow. They graze on seagrass and water plants, hours a day, very slowly.
Largest member of the order Sirenia, which also includes the dugong and the extinct Steller's sea cow.
Comes into Florida springs in winter, where the water stays warm year-round. They huddle in the warm spots when the rest of the bay gets cold.
aldo.size: About the size of a small car, in the water.
aldo.look: Large gray-brown aquatic mammal with a rounded body, paddle-shaped tail, two flippers, small bristled snout, tiny eyes. Wrinkles on the skin.
aldo.home: Coastal shallows, river mouths, springs in Florida and along the Gulf Coast.

facts: Floats on the back, holds rocks on the chest, cracks shellfish on the rock. Tools.
Has the densest fur of any mammal. They don't have blubber. The fur does the insulating.
Heaviest member of the weasel family. Smallest marine mammal. Both true at once.
aldo.size: About the size of a medium dog, but rounder.
aldo.look: Dark brown otter with a paler face and head, big webbed hind feet, small front paws, thick tail. Floats on its back. Lives most of life in the water.
aldo.home: Kelp forests and rocky coasts of California and Alaska. Rarely on land.

facts: Big shoulder hump made of muscle. That's how you tell a grizzly from a black bear at a distance.
Silver-tipped fur on adults — the grizzled part. Dish-shaped face, long claws.
A subspecies of the brown bear. The same animal as the brown bears in Alaska, Russia, and Europe.
aldo.size: About the size of a small car, standing.
aldo.look: Massive bear with a humped shoulder, long pale-tipped fur ranging from blonde to dark brown, dish-shaped face, long curved front claws.
aldo.home: Mountains, river valleys, alpine meadows. Alaska, the northern Rockies, parts of Idaho and Wyoming.

species.name: Gray Wolf
species.range: MN, WI, MI, ID, MT, WY

facts: Largest member of the dog family. Built like a coyote scaled up, with a heavier head.
Sometimes called the timber wolf. Lives in packs — a family group, mostly. They hunt as a team.
A wolf's howl carries miles. Other wolves answer, sometimes from beyond hearing for us.
aldo.size: About the size of a German Shepherd, with longer legs.
aldo.look: Large heavy canid with thick gray-brown fur (sometimes black or near-white), bushy tail, broad head, rounded ears, yellow eyes. Long legs, big paws.
aldo.home: Wilderness forests and tundra. Northern Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, the northern Rockies. Reintroduced where they were lost.

facts: Rams butt heads. The horns can weigh thirty pounds. The skull is built to take the hit.
Originally crossed from Siberia over the Bering land bridge. North America once had millions. Now hundreds of thousands.
Tan-brown body, white rump, big curling horns on the rams. Ewes have shorter horns that don't curl.
aldo.size: About the size of a medium deer.
aldo.look: Stocky tan-brown sheep with a white rump and muzzle, broad black-tipped horns. Rams have heavy curled horns; ewes have shorter, slimmer horns.
aldo.home: Rocky cliffs, alpine meadows, desert canyons of the Western mountains. They like steep escape terrain.

facts: Not actually a goat. Closer to antelopes than to barnyard goats, despite the name.
Stands on cliff ledges that look impossible. The hooves have soft pads in the center and hard rims around — they grip like rubber tires.
Pure white shaggy coat all year. Black horns, black hooves, black eyes. Looks like a small ghost on a rock face.
aldo.size: About the size of a large dog with extremely good balance.
aldo.look: White shaggy hoofed animal with a long beard, black horns curving slightly back, black hooves. Stocky build, sloping back, short tail.
aldo.home: Alpine cliffs and meadows above tree line in the Northwest mountains.

facts: Quills are modified hairs. Tens of thousands of them. They can't shoot — that's a story.
Second-largest rodent in North America, after the beaver.
Climbs trees and eats bark. Spends a lot of time up there, sleeping in branches.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog with a bristly back.
aldo.look: Stocky rodent covered in long brown-and-white quills mixed with fur. Small dark face, short legs, slow walk. The tail is short and quill-covered.
aldo.home: Forests across the north and the Rockies. They like a stand of trees with bark to chew.

facts: Not a fisher of fish. Mostly hunts small mammals — squirrels, rabbits, and porcupines, which is unusual.
Member of the weasel family. Larger than a marten, smaller than a wolverine. Long body, short legs.
Lives in dense northern and Appalachian forests. Quiet animal. Most people never see one.
aldo.size: About the size of a housecat with a longer body.
aldo.look: Long-bodied dark-brown weasel-relative with a bushy tail, small rounded ears, sharp face. The fur looks almost black on a wet day.
aldo.home: Boreal and Appalachian forests, especially with conifers and lots of cover.

facts: Wolverines look like small bears. They aren't. They're the largest member of the weasel family.
Live in the high mountains and remote north, far from people. Most people never see one and never will.
Eat almost anything they can find or kill. Carrion, marmots, small deer in deep snow.
aldo.size: About the size of a medium dog with a shorter body.
aldo.look: Stocky dark-brown weasel-relative with a pale stripe along each side, bushy tail, small rounded ears, broad furry feet. Powerful build.
aldo.home: Alpine meadows, boreal forests, remote wilderness in Alaska, Montana, Wyoming, and a few Colorado peaks.

facts: Males sing. Songs ten to twenty minutes long, repeated for hours. The songs change from year to year.
Up to fifty feet long, eighty thousand pounds. Long pectoral fins — almost a third of the body.
Breaches. Throws itself almost clear of the water, comes down on its side. Reasons not entirely clear, even to whale scientists.
aldo.size: About the size of a school bus, mostly underwater.
aldo.look: Huge dark-gray baleen whale with very long white-edged pectoral fins, knobbly head, broad flukes with white patterns underneath.
aldo.home: Open ocean and coastal waters off both US coasts and Hawaii. They migrate between cold feeding grounds and warm breeding grounds.

facts: Was thought extinct in 1979. A few were found in Wyoming in 1981 and bred up in captivity. They're being put back, slowly.
Prairie dogs are almost their entire diet. No prairie dogs, no ferrets.
Sandy-tan body, black mask across the eyes, black feet, black tail tip.
aldo.size: About the size of a small housecat with a longer body.
aldo.look: Long slender weasel with a sandy-buff body, dark mask through the eyes, black feet, black-tipped tail. Pointed face, small rounded ears.
aldo.home: Prairie dog colonies on the Great Plains. They live in the burrows.

facts: Most abundant native tree in eastern North America. The Forest Service counted.
Sometimes called swamp maple or soft maple. Grows in wet ground better than most trees.
Red flowers in early spring. Red samaras — those helicopter seeds — by June. Red leaves in fall. Red, red, and red.
aldo.size: About the size of a small water tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Medium-large deciduous tree with three- or five-lobed leaves, red flowers in early spring before leaves, paired winged seeds, smooth gray bark on young trees and ridged dark bark on old ones.
aldo.home: Forests, yards, and especially wet ground — swamps, river bottoms, drainages. Eastern half of the country.

facts: Some white oaks alive today are older than four hundred years.
Leaves have rounded lobes — no points or bristles. The acorns mature in one season instead of two.
Pale gray bark, often with a whitish look. That's the white in the name.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn at full grown.
aldo.look: Big spreading oak with rounded-lobed leaves, pale gray flaking bark, light brown acorns with shallow caps. The crown is broad and rounded.
aldo.home: Forests and parks across the eastern half of the country. They like deep soil.

facts: Five soft needles per bundle. The only eastern pine with five.
Once the tallest tree in the eastern forest. Logged hard in the 1800s. They're growing back.
The cones are long and slim, often with white pitch on them.
aldo.size: About the size of a small radio tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall straight pine with soft blue-green needles in bundles of five, long slender cones, smooth gray bark on young trees that gets ridged with age. Branches in horizontal whorls.
aldo.home: Forests, hillsides, and old fields across the Northeast and Great Lakes.

facts: The leaf on the Canadian flag. The same kind of leaf shows up across the northern US.
Sap is the source of maple syrup. It takes about forty gallons of sap to make one gallon of syrup. Slow work.
Fall color is the brilliant orange and red the eastern hardwoods are famous for.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn at full grown.
aldo.look: Big deciduous tree with five-lobed leaves that have smooth-edged points (not toothed). Smooth gray bark on young trees, plated and shaggy on old ones. Paired winged seeds.
aldo.home: Northern hardwood forests, sugar bushes, parks, and yards in the Northeast and Great Lakes.

facts: Second most common tree in the country, after the red maple.
Native to the southeast. Grows fast and straight. The southern timber industry leans on it.
Three needles per bundle, six to nine inches long. Cones with sharp prickles.
aldo.size: About the size of a small radio tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall pine with long bright-green needles in bundles of three, scaly gray-brown bark in irregular plates, long pointed cones with sharp prickles.
aldo.home: Lowlands and pine plantations of the southeastern coastal plain, Texas to Delaware.

facts: Not actually a cedar. A juniper. Sometimes called pencil cedar — the wood used to be cut for pencils.
Female trees grow blue berries — actually little cones — that birds eat all winter.
Smells sweet when you crush a sprig. Old fence posts of this wood last forever.
aldo.size: About the size of a small house when full-grown, more often the size of a shed.
aldo.look: Evergreen tree with scale-like green or blue-green foliage, fibrous reddish-brown bark that peels in strips, blue waxy berry-like cones (on female trees only).
aldo.home: Old fields, fence rows, edges, dry hillsides across the eastern half of the country.

facts: The bark flakes off in patches. White, cream, and tan all on the same trunk. From a distance, the upper branches look painted.
Among the largest hardwoods in eastern North America. Some old trees have hollow trunks big enough to stand inside.
Round seed balls hang on through winter. They look like Christmas ornaments by January.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn, with patchy white bark.
aldo.look: Massive deciduous tree with mottled bark — patches of white, cream, gray, and tan. Big maple-like leaves. Round, fuzzy seed balls dangle from long stems.
aldo.home: Riverbanks, bottomlands, floodplains. Sometimes parks and streets.

facts: Five-pointed leaves shaped like a star. Or like a maple leaf with extra points.
Spiky seed balls drop in fall and stay through winter. They cluster underfoot in a way that's hard to ignore.
Fall color goes through yellow, orange, red, and purple, sometimes all on the same tree at once.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall deciduous tree with five-pointed star-shaped leaves, spiky round seed balls, gray bark with corky ridges. Brilliant multicolored fall foliage.
aldo.home: Forests and yards across the southeast and central US. Likes deep moist soil.

facts: Not a true fir, despite the name. Its own kind of tree. The cones tell you — bracts that look like the back legs and tail of a mouse hiding under the scales.
Among the tallest trees on the continent. Coast Douglas-firs over three hundred feet are still around in old groves.
Soft flat needles all the way around the twig. Sweet citrusy smell when you crush them.
aldo.size: About the size of a small radio tower, in old groves.
aldo.look: Tall conifer with soft flat needles, hanging cones with three-pronged bracts sticking out (mouse-tail bracts), thick deeply furrowed bark on old trees.
aldo.home: Mountain forests of the West, especially the Pacific Northwest. Also dry interior mountains as far east as the Rockies.

facts: The bark of an old ponderosa smells like vanilla or butterscotch. Stick your nose into a crack on a sunny day and check.
Most widely distributed pine in North America.
Three needles per bundle, long and tufted. The plates of old bark fit together like puzzle pieces.
aldo.size: About the size of a small radio tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall pine with long needles in bundles of three, large prickly cones, orange-brown to cinnamon plated bark on old trees that fits together in jigsaw pieces.
aldo.home: Dry montane forests across the western US, foothills and interior mountains.

facts: The leaves shake in even a small breeze. The leafstalk is flat and at right angles to the blade — that's why.
Whole groves are often one organism. The trees grow from a shared root system. The biggest known clone covers a hundred acres.
White bark with black scars. Gold leaves in fall. A grove turning at once is the kind of thing that stops you in the road.
aldo.size: About the size of a small water tower.
aldo.look: Deciduous tree with smooth chalky-white bark scarred with black, round leaves that tremble in any breeze, golden fall color.
aldo.home: Mountain slopes, burned-over country, ridges across the northern and western US.

facts: Evergreen. The leaves stay on through winter. New leaves push the old ones off in spring.
Massive trees with horizontal branches that can spread wider than the tree is tall. Spanish moss often hangs from them in long gray streamers.
Iconic of the deep South. Old plantation oaks, town squares, oak alleys.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn, but wider than tall.
aldo.look: Evergreen oak with leathery oval leaves, smooth-edged or slightly toothed. Massive horizontal branches, deeply furrowed dark bark, small acorns. Often draped with Spanish moss.
aldo.home: Coastal southeastern US, parks, streets, plantations. They like sandy soils within a hundred miles of the coast.

facts: Big trees. Old leaves underfoot. Cool ravines, where the air stays a few degrees cooler than the ridge above.
State tree of Pennsylvania.
Tiny cones, less than an inch long. Soft flat needles in two flat rows. The whole branch looks feathery.
aldo.size: About the size of a small water tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall conifer with short flat needles arranged in two rows, very small cones, deeply furrowed dark bark on old trees, drooping leader on the top of the tree.
aldo.home: Cool moist forests and ravines, mostly in the Northeast and the Appalachian Mountains.

facts: Smooth gray bark you can't help but want to touch. People have carved into it for centuries. The scars never heal.
Old leaves stay on the tree all winter. They turn copper and rattle in the wind, a paper sound.
Triangular nuts in spiny husks. Bears, squirrels, and turkeys eat them in fall.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall deciduous tree with smooth pale gray bark, oblong toothed leaves, long pointed buds, small triangular beechnuts in spiny husks. Coppery dead leaves stay on through winter.
aldo.home: Rich shaded forests across the eastern half of the country. They like deep soil and an old canopy.

facts: A conifer that drops its needles in fall. That's what the bald means.
Grows knees — woody bumps that come up out of the swamp around the trunk. Why is still debated.
Coppery-orange needles in October before they fall. A swamp full of bald cypress in autumn is something.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn, often standing in water.
aldo.look: Tall deciduous conifer with feathery soft needles, fluted base, woody knees rising from the water around it, small round cones, fibrous reddish bark.
aldo.home: Swamps, river bottoms, blackwater bayous of the southeastern US.

facts: Bark peels off in white papery strips. People have used it for canoes, baskets, even paper.
Often the first tree to come back after a fire in the northern woods.
Yellow leaves in fall. Against dark conifers, a paper birch in October is hard to miss.
aldo.size: About the size of a tall flagpole at full grown.
aldo.look: Slender deciduous tree with chalky-white peeling bark marked by horizontal black lines, oval toothed leaves, small drooping seed catkins.
aldo.home: Northern forests, lakeshores, burned-over land across the upper US.

facts: The tallest hardwood east of the Rockies. Grows up to a hundred and sixty feet in old cove forests.
Yellow-green flowers in spring shaped like tulips. Up high in the canopy. You usually find them on the ground first.
The leaf has a flat top instead of a point — like someone cut the tip off.
aldo.size: About the size of a small radio tower in old groves.
aldo.look: Tall deciduous tree with leaves that look like a four-lobed silhouette of a tulip. Yellow-green tulip-shaped flowers high in the canopy. Smooth gray bark on young trees, deeply furrowed on old.
aldo.home: Rich Appalachian and eastern hardwood forests. Cove forests especially.

facts: Tallest trees on Earth. Some over three hundred and seventy feet.
Lives twelve hundred to eighteen hundred years, sometimes longer.
Needs the fog. Coastal fog drips down off the canopy and waters the roots in the dry season.
aldo.size: About the size of a thirty-story building.
aldo.look: Massive evergreen conifer with thick reddish furrowed bark, flat short needles, small cones. Trunks rise straight up two hundred feet before branching.
aldo.home: Coastal fog belt forests of northern California and a sliver of southern Oregon.

facts: Most massive tree on Earth by volume. Not the tallest — the coast redwood is taller. The biggest by sheer wood.
Some are over three thousand years old. John Muir called them Big Trees.
Cinnamon-colored bark a foot or two thick. Almost fireproof. They've survived fires that took everything else.
aldo.size: About the size of a small lighthouse in girth.
aldo.look: Massive evergreen conifer with thick spongy reddish-cinnamon bark, scale-like blue-green foliage, small egg-shaped cones, enormous trunks that swell at the base.
aldo.home: Mountain groves at moderate elevation in the Sierra Nevada of California.

facts: Doesn't grow its first arm until it's around seventy years old. They take their time.
Up to forty feet tall. Some live over a hundred and fifty years.
White flowers open at night in late spring. The state wildflower of Arizona.
aldo.size: About the size of a telephone pole, with arms.
aldo.look: Tall columnar cactus with vertical pleated ribs, sharp spines, and stout upward-curving arms on older plants. Waxy white flowers ringed at the top in late spring.
aldo.home: Sonoran Desert in Arizona, parts of southern California, and northern Mexico.

facts: Acorns the size of golf balls, with fringed caps that cover most of the nut. Biggest acorns of any oak.
Thick corky bark. Built to survive prairie fires.
Lives where the prairie meets the forest. Tough tree.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn at full grown, with a wide spread.
aldo.look: Big spreading oak with deeply lobed leaves, very large acorns with fringed mossy caps, thick corky deeply furrowed bark.
aldo.home: Prairie groves, oak savannas, river edges across the central US.

facts: The blue is from a waxy bloom on the needles. New growth in spring is the bluest. Older needles are duller.
Native to the Rocky Mountains. Common in yards everywhere — people plant it for the color.
Sharp four-sided needles. They prick. That's how you tell a spruce from a fir.
aldo.size: About the size of a small water tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Conifer with stiff sharp four-sided needles ranging from green to pale silvery-blue, pendant cones, conical shape, gray scaly bark.
aldo.home: Streambanks and moist mountain slopes of the central and southern Rockies. Also planted everywhere.

facts: A yucca, not a tree in the usual sense. The trunk is fibrous, not woody.
Lives a hundred and fifty years or more. Some are likely older than that.
Cream-colored flowers in spring on stalks at the branch tips. Pollinated almost only by yucca moths.
aldo.size: About the size of a small tree, with stiff arms and spikes.
aldo.look: Tree-like yucca with stout fibrous trunk, branches ending in clusters of long stiff spiky leaves, cream flowers in spring on tall stalks.
aldo.home: Mojave Desert in southern California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah.

facts: Spends years as a tuft of needles on the ground — the grass stage — before sending up a trunk. Like the tree is taking a long, slow breath.
Needles can be over a foot long. Bundles of three.
Native to the southeastern coastal plain. The longleaf forest used to cover ninety million acres. Most of it is gone now.
aldo.size: About the size of a small radio tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall pine with very long bright green needles in bundles of three, large cones, scaly bark in irregular plates. Young trees look like a tuft of needles before forming a trunk.
aldo.home: Sandy coastal plains and pine flatwoods of the Southeast.

facts: The hulls of the walnuts stain everything. Hands, sidewalks, the bottom of the dog. Permanent until it wears off.
Long compound leaves with many small leaflets. Among the last trees to leaf out in spring.
Roots release a chemical that keeps many other plants from growing under the tree. Tomatoes especially won't grow there.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall deciduous tree with long compound leaves of many leaflets, dark deeply furrowed bark, round green husks holding hard-shelled walnuts. Yellow-brown twigs with chambered pith.
aldo.home: Rich forests, river bottoms, yards across the eastern US.

facts: Not a true cedar. A relative of the cypress. The smell when you crush a sprig is the same one you find in a cedar chest.
Bark peels in long fibrous strips. Native peoples of the Pacific Northwest used it for clothing, rope, baskets, canoes — most of life.
Lives a long time. Old trees over a thousand years old still stand in the Olympic and Cascade rainforests.
aldo.size: About the size of a small water tower at full grown.
aldo.look: Tall evergreen conifer with scale-like flat green sprays, fibrous reddish-brown bark in long vertical strips, small upright cones, drooping branch tips.
aldo.home: Coastal and interior rainforests of the Pacific Northwest. Wet places.

facts: Largest spruce in the world. Some over three hundred feet, with trunks sixteen feet across.
Wood is light, strong, and resonant. Was used for early airplane frames. Still used for guitar tops.
Sharp flat needles, easy to identify by feel. Run a hand along a branch and you'll know.
aldo.size: About the size of a small radio tower in coastal old growth.
aldo.look: Massive evergreen conifer with sharp flat green needles, papery cones with thin scales, scaly purplish-gray bark, drooping outer branches.
aldo.home: Coastal rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, from northern California to Alaska. Within fog reach.

facts: Vase-shaped — the trunk rises and the branches arch out and then up, like a wineglass. They used to line American main streets.
Dutch elm disease wiped out most of them in the twentieth century. New disease-resistant varieties are slowly bringing them back.
Leaves are oval with sharp double-toothed edges and an uneven base — one side meets the stem lower than the other.
aldo.size: About the size of a small barn at full grown, taller than wide.
aldo.look: Tall deciduous tree with a classic vase shape, double-toothed asymmetrical oval leaves, gray ridged bark, small papery winged seeds in early spring.
aldo.home: Bottomland forests, riverbanks, streets in the eastern half of the country.

facts: Among the oldest living things on Earth. One in California is over five thousand years old.
Grows on high windy ridges where almost nothing else can. The harder the place, the longer they last.
Trunks are gnarled and twisted. Often more dead wood than living. The living strip keeps the tree going.
aldo.size: About the size of a knotted old shed.
aldo.look: Short twisted conifer with very long-lived gnarled wood, short bottlebrush-like needles in bundles of five, small purple-tinted cones with bristles. Often half-dead with a single living strip.
aldo.home: High mountain ridges in California, Nevada, and Utah, near or above timberline.

facts: Stilt roots arch out of the trunk and prop the tree up in saltwater. The whole forest stands on its own legs.
Seeds sprout while still on the tree. The seedling drops point-first into the mud and roots before the tide takes it.
Tolerates salt by filtering most of it out at the roots. The leaves shed what gets through.
aldo.size: About the size of a small house, more often the size of a hedge.
aldo.look: Evergreen coastal tree with arched stilt roots, glossy oval leaves, small yellow flowers, and long pencil-like seedlings dangling from the branches.
aldo.home: Coastal saltwater shorelines and tidal flats in southern Florida, the Gulf Coast, and the Caribbean.

facts: Break the stem and white sap leaks out. The sap is bitter and toxic. Monarchs eat the leaves anyway, and become bitter themselves.
Pink globe of small flowers, sweet-smelling, full of bees in July.
Pods split open in fall to release seeds with long silky hairs. The wind carries them far. Some get stuck in your sweater.
aldo.size: About the size of a tall summer weed, waist-high.
aldo.look: Stout perennial with broad oval leaves growing in pairs along the stem, milky sap, dome-shaped clusters of pink-purple flowers, big warty seed pods.
aldo.home: Old fields, roadsides, sunny edges across the eastern and central US.

facts: Yellow ray petals around a dark domed center. The center is the black eye.
Native to the eastern and central US, but now grows in all forty-eight contiguous states. Roadsides everywhere.
A sunflower relative. Same family. The flowers are smaller and there are usually a lot of them at once.
aldo.size: About the size of a coffee mug at the flower head.
aldo.look: Sturdy perennial with rough hairy stems and leaves, daisy-like flowers with golden-yellow rays and a dark brown-purple central cone.
aldo.home: Fields, meadows, roadsides, prairies. Almost any sunny disturbed ground.

facts: The petals droop back from the dark spiky center, like the flower is sighing in the heat.
Native to the eastern and central US, especially the Ozarks and the Mississippi-Ohio Valley.
Goldfinches strip the seeds out of the dried cones in late summer.
aldo.size: About the size of a teacup at the flower head.
aldo.look: Tall prairie perennial with rough lance-shaped leaves and pink-purple petals drooping from a coppery-brown spiky cone.
aldo.home: Prairies, meadows, gardens across the eastern and central US.

facts: Yellow flower head, then a clock of seeds, then nothing. The whole thing happens fast.
Every part is edible. Greens, flowers, even the roots.
Each puffball seed is its own parachute. They go where the wind takes them, sometimes for miles.
aldo.size: About the size of a wine cork at the flower head.
aldo.look: Low rosette of jagged-toothed leaves, single hollow stem with milky sap, bright yellow flower head, white puffball of feathery seeds.
aldo.home: Lawns, sidewalks, ditches, fields. Anywhere the soil has been disturbed even a little.

facts: Heart-shaped leaves and small purple flowers, low to the ground. Easy to walk past.
The flowers and leaves are both edible. People used to make candied violets out of the petals.
Spreads quickly. A single plant becomes a patch in a few seasons.
aldo.size: About the size of a small coin at the flower.
aldo.look: Low perennial with heart-shaped scalloped leaves and small five-petaled flowers, deep purple to white. The lower petal is often striped to guide bees in.
aldo.home: Lawns, woods, edges, damp shady ground across the eastern half of the country.

facts: Late-summer color along almost every roadside. Yellow plumes, all at once, all over.
People often blame goldenrod for hay fever. It's not the culprit — that's mostly ragweed, which blooms at the same time.
Bees, wasps, butterflies, soldier beetles — a goldenrod patch in September is busy.
aldo.size: About the size of a tall summer weed, waist-high.
aldo.look: Tall perennial with narrow lance-shaped leaves and many small yellow flowers grouped in plume-like or flat-topped clusters at the top of the stem.
aldo.home: Fields, prairies, roadsides, edges across the country.

facts: A flat white umbrella of tiny flowers. Often a single dark purple floret in the center, like a fly on a tablecloth.
Originally from Europe and Asia. Naturalized everywhere now. Sometimes called wild carrot — same species as the carrot in your garden, just a wild ancestor.
When the flower is done, the umbrella curls up into a bird's-nest shape full of seeds.
aldo.size: About the size of a saucer at the flower head.
aldo.look: Tall biennial with finely cut feathery leaves and a flat lacy umbrella of small white flowers. Sometimes a single dark purple floret in the center.
aldo.home: Roadsides, fields, disturbed ground across the country.

facts: Pink to red pom-pom of tiny flowers. Bumblebees especially love it.
Native to Europe, planted everywhere as livestock feed. Now it's in lawns and roadsides everywhere.
Three leaflets, often with a pale V mark on each. The four-leaf clovers people look for are this species' cousins.
aldo.size: About the size of a quarter at the flower head.
aldo.look: Low perennial with three-part leaves, each leaflet often marked with a pale V. Round pink-to-red flower heads on long stems.
aldo.home: Lawns, fields, pastures, roadsides everywhere.

facts: The colorful tip isn't the flower. It's a cluster of bright red-orange leaves around small green flowers tucked inside.
Partly parasitic. Sends its roots out to tap into the roots of nearby plants for water and nutrients.
