Mountain meadows in the West, full of paintbrush in early summer, look like the ground is on fire in patches.
aldo.size: About the size of a small paintbrush, in clumps.
aldo.look: Slender wildflower with narrow leaves and a cluster of bright red, orange, or yellow bracts at the top, surrounding small greenish flowers.
aldo.home: Mountain meadows, sagebrush flats, prairie hillsides across the West.

facts: State flower of Texas, in all of its bluebonnet versions. This one is the most common.
Spring fields in central Texas turn entirely blue. People stop their cars on the side of the road for it.
A lupine. Same family as the western lupines, with palmate leaves like a hand.
aldo.size: About the size of a small ice cream cone at the flower spike.
aldo.look: Low annual with palmate leaves of five to seven leaflets and short spikes of deep blue pea-shaped flowers, often tipped with white.
aldo.home: Prairies, roadsides, and old fields in central Texas, mostly.

facts: State flower of California since 1903.
Cup-shaped, four orange petals, on a thin stem. Closes at night and on cloudy days.
Hillsides in southern California turn solid orange in a wet spring.
aldo.size: About the size of a shot glass at the flower.
aldo.look: Slender annual or perennial with finely divided blue-green leaves and bright orange cup-shaped flowers with four silky petals on long stems.
aldo.home: Hills, fields, roadsides, sandy slopes across California and the Southwest.

facts: Three of everything. Three leaves, three petals, three sepals. The name itself comes from the Latin for three.
Spring ephemeral. Up, blooming, gone, all before the trees fully leaf out.
Picking a trillium hurts the plant for years. The whole leaf is also the food-maker for next year. Without it, the corm starves.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dinner plate at the leaves.
aldo.look: Spring perennial with a single whorl of three broad leaves at the top of the stem and a single three-petaled flower above them. Flowers white, pink, red, or yellow depending on species.
aldo.home: Rich shaded hardwood forests across the eastern half of the country.

facts: Red and yellow hanging bell with five spurs sticking up. A hummingbird's flower — the spurs hold nectar at the tip.
Hybridizes easily with garden columbines. Wild colonies near gardens often show mixed colors.
Likes rocky woods and cliff ledges. Spring blooms come early in the eastern forests.
aldo.size: About the size of a small thimble at the flower.
aldo.look: Slender perennial with delicate compound leaves of three-lobed leaflets. Hanging flowers with red outside, yellow inside, five long spurs pointing upward.
aldo.home: Rocky woods, cliffs, ledges, and shady banks across the eastern US.

facts: A milkweed, but the sap is more clear than milky. Different from common milkweed in that.
Bright orange clusters, sometimes yellow. Monarchs and many other butterflies use it.
Long taproot. Hard to transplant. Easier to start from seed.
aldo.size: About the size of a baseball glove at the flower clusters.
aldo.look: Sturdy perennial with narrow alternate leaves and flat-topped clusters of bright orange or yellow flowers. Hairy stems, narrow seed pods.
aldo.home: Dry fields, prairies, sandy roadsides across the eastern and central US.

facts: First plant up after a fire. Tall pink spikes by the thousands across burned-over country in summer.
Common across the north and the western mountains. Especially abundant in Alaska and the Rockies.
Flowers open from the bottom of the spike up. By the time the top is blooming, the bottom is going to seed.
aldo.size: About the size of a tall summer weed, waist-high or higher.
aldo.look: Tall perennial with narrow willow-like leaves and a long spike of bright pink-purple four-petaled flowers. Long thin seed pods that release silky cottony seeds.
aldo.home: Burned-over country, clearings, roadsides, mountain slopes across the northern and western US.

facts: Snap a stem, red sap leaks out. That's the blood. The Lenape used it as dye.
Single white flower wrapped in a single curled leaf when it first comes up. The leaf opens like a hand later.
Spring ephemeral. The flowers are open for only a few days before the petals fall.
aldo.size: About the size of a small biscuit at the flower.
aldo.look: Spring perennial with a single deeply lobed gray-green leaf wrapped around the stem at first, and a single pure white flower with eight to twelve petals and a yellow center.
aldo.home: Rich hardwood forests, especially on slopes, across the eastern half of the country.

facts: The lower petal is shaped like a slipper, or a small sac. Bees crawl in and have to push past the pollen on the way out.
Several species in the eastern and northern US — yellow, pink, white, and the showy lady's slipper, which has both pink and white in one flower.
Slow to grow. Some take years to flower for the first time. Don't dig them up — they almost never survive transplant.
aldo.size: About the size of a small egg at the slipper.
aldo.look: Tall woodland orchid with broad ribbed leaves and a single (or paired) flower with a pouch-shaped lower petal in pink, yellow, or white.
aldo.home: Bogs, rich forests, swamp edges across the northern and eastern US.

facts: All white. No green at all. It doesn't make its own food — it gets it from fungi connected to tree roots, like a quiet thief.
Sometimes called ghost plant or corpse plant. The whole thing turns black when it's done.
Comes up in dim woods after summer rain. Easy to walk past, then once you see one you see a dozen.
aldo.size: About the size of a small candle.
aldo.look: Pale waxy-white plant with no green, stem topped by a single nodding bell-shaped flower that turns upward as the seed pod develops.
aldo.home: Dim shaded forest floors with deep leaf litter, mostly in the eastern US.

facts: Eats insects. The trap snaps shut when something brushes the trigger hairs on the inside, twice within a few seconds.
Native only to a small patch of the Carolinas. Thirty-mile radius around Wilmington, more or less.
Most of what you see in stores comes from cultivation. Wild populations are protected — and at risk from poaching.
aldo.size: About the size of a quarter at each trap.
aldo.look: Small carnivorous plant with paired hinged trap leaves edged with bristles and trigger hairs on the inner surfaces. Small white flowers on a tall stalk.
aldo.home: Wet pine savannas and bogs in a small area of North and South Carolina.

facts: Yellow flowers on long stems, woolly silver-gray leaves at the base. The leaves stay close to the ground to keep cool.
Blooms most of the year in the southwest deserts when there's enough rain.
Toxic to livestock. Sheep and cattle leave it alone, which is part of why it lasts in grazed country.
aldo.size: About the size of a coffee mug at the flower head.
aldo.look: Low desert perennial with a basal rosette of woolly gray-green leaves and tall slender stems each topped with a single bright yellow daisy-like flower.
aldo.home: Deserts, sandy washes, roadsides across the Southwest.

facts: Palmate leaves, like a hand laid flat. Tall spikes of pea-shaped flowers, blue or purple or sometimes white.
Roots fix nitrogen. They make poor soil better. Many lupines pioneer disturbed ground.
Pollinated by bumblebees mostly. The flowers are built so a bee has to push down on the lower petal to get to the nectar.
aldo.size: About the size of a small ear of corn at the flower spike.
aldo.look: Perennial or annual with palmate leaves of five to many leaflets, tall spikes of pea-shaped purple, blue, or white flowers, and small fuzzy seed pods.
aldo.home: Mountain meadows, prairies, forest openings, roadsides across the West.

facts: Petals swept back behind the flower, like the head of a small dart in flight.
Pollinated mostly by bumblebees. They land on the flower upside down and buzz the pollen out.
Spring ephemeral in moist meadows and prairies. Up, blooming, gone in a few weeks.
aldo.size: About the size of a small spoon at each flower.
aldo.look: Spring perennial with a basal rosette of smooth oblong leaves and a leafless stem topped by several nodding flowers with petals swept back behind a yellow-and-purple beak of fused stamens.
aldo.home: Moist meadows, prairies, open woods. Across most of the country in scattered species.

facts: Jack is a small spike inside the hood. The hood is the pulpit. The whole arrangement is one flower.
Three-part leaves stand above the flower. Sometimes one leaf, sometimes two.
Fall fruit is a tight cluster of bright red berries on the spike. The leaves are gone by then.
aldo.size: About the size of a small candle holder at the flower.
aldo.look: Spring woodland perennial with one or two three-parted leaves on tall stalks and a hooded flower — a striped green or purple sheath curling over an upright spike (the jack).
aldo.home: Rich shaded forests, swamps, wooded wetlands across the eastern US.

facts: State wildflower of Arizona. Blooms only on the saguaro, mostly in May and June.
Flowers open at night and close by midday. Bats pollinate them in the dark, then bees and birds finish the job in the morning.
Each flower lasts about a day. A saguaro can have a hundred buds at a time, opening in shifts.
aldo.size: About the size of a small teacup, on top of the cactus.
aldo.look: Waxy white flower with a yellow center, ringed with many petals, opening at the tip of a saguaro arm. Long stamens and a thick green base.
aldo.home: Top of saguaro cacti in the Sonoran Desert in Arizona.

facts: First wildflower of spring in the northeast wetlands. Comes up while there's still snow.
Generates its own heat. The flower can melt snow around itself. Few plants can do this.
Smells like a skunk when you crush a leaf. That's where the name comes from. Flies and beetles like the smell, and pollinate it.
aldo.size: About the size of a folded leather glove at the flower hood.
aldo.look: Low wetland perennial with a streaked maroon-and-green hood-shaped flower (spathe) wrapping a knobby spike (spadix). Big cabbage-like leaves come up after the flower.
aldo.home: Wet woods, swamps, and seeps across the Northeast and Great Lakes.

facts: The migration is the famous part. Eastern monarchs travel down to a few small mountain valleys in central Mexico every fall. The same trees, year after year, even though no individual butterfly has ever been there before.
Caterpillars eat only milkweed. The toxins make the butterfly poisonous to most predators.
Wings about four inches across. Orange with thick black veins and a white-spotted black border.
aldo.size: About the size of an open paperback at the wings.
aldo.look: Large orange-and-black butterfly with thick black wing veins and white spots along the black borders. Males have a small black scent patch on each hindwing.
aldo.home: Fields, gardens, roadsides, anywhere with milkweed. Across the country in summer; overwintering in central Mexico and coastal California.

facts: Most common honeybee in the world. Apis mellifera — Latin for honey-bearing.
Not native to the Americas. Brought over with European settlers in the 1600s.
A hive is one colony, mostly sisters, with a single queen. They communicate where the flowers are by dancing.
aldo.size: About the size of a small almond.
aldo.look: Slender hairy bee with a fuzzy golden-brown thorax and a banded yellow-and-brown abdomen. Wings clear, six legs with pollen baskets on the hind pair.
aldo.home: Anywhere flowers grow — gardens, orchards, fields, meadows. Hives in tree hollows, walls, or beekeeper boxes.

facts: Most common bumblebee across the eastern half of the country. Big, fuzzy, hard to miss.
Lives in country, suburbs, and even cities. They use everything from wildflowers to tomato plants.
Buzz-pollinates. Holds onto the flower and vibrates the pollen out. Honeybees can't do this.
aldo.size: About the size of a hazelnut.
aldo.look: Round fuzzy bumblebee with a yellow band on the front of the thorax, a yellow band at the front of the abdomen, the rest black. Big black eyes, short tongue.
aldo.home: Gardens, meadows, suburbs, fields across the eastern and central US.

facts: Sometimes called the cosmopolitan. They live almost everywhere on Earth, except Antarctica.
Some years there are millions in big migrations across the western US. Other years almost none.
Orange and brown with black-and-white wingtips. Underside dull and patterned for camouflage.
aldo.size: About the size of a credit card at the wings.
aldo.look: Medium butterfly with orange-and-brown wings, black markings, white spots near the black wingtips. Underside marbled brown, black, and pale orange with eyespots.
aldo.home: Open fields, gardens, deserts, roadsides — almost anywhere. Across the country.

facts: Big yellow butterfly with thick black tiger stripes and long swallow tails. Hard to mistake for anything else, in its range.
Two or three broods through the year, spring through fall.
Females come in two forms — yellow like the male, or all black. The black ones mimic the toxic pipevine swallowtail.
aldo.size: About the size of an open paperback at the wings.
aldo.look: Large butterfly. Yellow wings with bold black stripes, black wing borders with yellow spots and blue scaling, long tail extensions on hindwings. Some females are entirely black.
aldo.home: Forests, edges, gardens, river bottoms across the eastern half of the country.

facts: One of the few dragonflies that migrates. Some travel from Canada to Mexico and back over generations.
Among the largest and most common dragonflies in North America.
Bright green thorax, blue or pinkish-purple abdomen, big eyes that meet on top of the head.
aldo.size: About the size of a popsicle stick.
aldo.look: Big dragonfly with a bright green thorax, long blue (male) or purplish (female) abdomen, large compound eyes meeting on top, clear wings with a slight golden tint.
aldo.home: Ponds, marshes, slow rivers across the country.

facts: Three black spots on each red wing cover, and one shared across the seam. Seven spots, hence the name.
Originally European. Released in the US to control aphids, and now established almost everywhere.
Eats aphids by the dozen. Both adults and larvae are predators.
aldo.size: About the size of a pencil eraser.
aldo.look: Small round red beetle with a black head edged in white and seven black dots on the wing covers. Short antennae, six tiny black legs.
aldo.home: Gardens, fields, meadows wherever aphids are.

facts: Lime-green wings with long curling tails, four and a half inches across. Looks more like a sea creature than a moth.
Adults have no functioning mouth. They live a week, mate, and die. The whole point of the adult is the next generation.
Comes to porch lights at night in the eastern woods, late spring through summer.
aldo.size: About the size of an open hand at the wings.
aldo.look: Large moth with pale green wings, long curling hindwing tails, small eye-like marks on each wing, a pinkish-purple stripe along the front of each forewing, white feathery body.
aldo.home: Deciduous forests across the eastern half of the country.

facts: The praying part is the front legs held up like folded hands. They're for grabbing, not praying.
Can turn the head almost halfway around — the only insect that can.
Female sometimes eats the male after mating. Sometimes during. Not always, but often enough to be famous.
aldo.size: About the size of a green crayon, with arms.
aldo.look: Long slender insect, usually bright green or pale brown, with a triangular head, big compound eyes, long thorax, and long folded forelegs lined with spines.
aldo.home: Gardens, meadows, weedy fields, roadside brush. Late summer through fall.

facts: State butterfly of Oklahoma and New Jersey.
Caterpillars eat parsley, dill, fennel, and carrot leaves. Often found right in the garden.
Black wings with two rows of yellow spots, blue scaling on the hindwing, and a small orange-and-blue eye-spot near each tail.
aldo.size: About the size of a postcard at the wings.
aldo.look: Mostly black butterfly with two bands of yellow spots, blue dusting on the hindwing, orange eye-spot near each tail. Females have less yellow and more blue.
aldo.home: Gardens, fields, meadows, open country across the eastern half of the country.

facts: The light comes from a chemical reaction in the abdomen. Almost no heat — just light. The most efficient light there is.
Each species has its own flash pattern. Males flash to females. Females answer from the grass.
Most common firefly in North America is the big dipper firefly. Slow J-shaped flash, low over the lawn at dusk.
aldo.size: About the size of a piece of rice, with a glow.
aldo.look: Soft-bodied beetle, dark brown or black with a red and yellow shield over the head. Pale or yellow segments at the tip of the abdomen — the light organ.
aldo.home: Yards, meadows, woodland edges, anywhere with damp soil and tall grass for the larvae. Eastern half of the country mostly.

facts: The caterpillar of the Isabella tiger moth. Black at the ends, rusty in the middle. People say the size of the rusty band predicts the winter. It doesn't.
Spends winter as a caterpillar. Freezes solid. Thaws out in spring and finishes growing.
Crawling across roads in fall is what people see most. The moth they turn into is plain pale orange and barely noticed.
aldo.size: About the size of a cigar stub, fuzzy.
aldo.look: Stout fuzzy caterpillar with stiff bristles, black at both ends and a rusty-orange band across the middle. Curls up tight when touched.
aldo.home: Fields, roadsides, yards across the country. Most visible in fall, when they're walking around looking for a place to overwinter.

facts: Spends thirteen or seventeen years underground as a nymph, eating tree roots. Then comes up all at once with millions of others.
Red eyes, black body, orange wing veins. Hard to mistake for the annual cicadas, which are green-and-black.
When a brood emerges, the noise is constant for weeks. Eighty decibels in some woods. Then the cicadas die and it's quiet again for thirteen or seventeen years.
aldo.size: About the size of a thumb-sized leaf with wings.
aldo.look: Stout black-bodied insect with bright red eyes, orange-veined transparent wings, and broad orange-tinted underparts.
aldo.home: Eastern deciduous forests, suburbs, yards. Specific broods come up in specific years across mapped regions.

facts: Sometimes called the writing spider for the zigzag stripe of silk down the middle of the web. Nobody is sure why she puts it there.
Big yellow-and-black abdomen, white face. The Latin name means gilded silver-face.
Female is several times the size of the male. He often gets eaten after mating.
aldo.size: About the size of a half-dollar, with long legs.
aldo.look: Large orb-weaving spider with a bright yellow-and-black patterned abdomen, mostly white head, long banded black-and-orange legs. Web has a white zigzag of silk down the middle.
aldo.home: Gardens, meadows, fields, weedy edges. Web hung between tall plants in late summer.

facts: An eastern subspecies of the black swallowtail. Same butterfly, more or less, with slightly stronger blue scaling on the hindwings.
Caterpillars eat the carrot family — parsley, dill, fennel, Queen Anne's lace. Often in the herb bed.
Black with two rows of yellow spots, blue scaling on the hindwing, and small orange-and-blue eyes near the tails.
aldo.size: About the size of a postcard at the wings.
aldo.look: Mostly black butterfly with two bands of yellow spots, vivid blue scaling on the hindwings, small orange-and-blue eye-spots near each tail. Females have less yellow and more blue.
aldo.home: Gardens, fields, meadows in the eastern half of the country.

facts: Largest native moth in North America. Wingspan over six inches in big females.
Brown wings with reddish bands and a crescent eyespot on each one. Big white-and-black furry body.
Caterpillars are bright green with bumps in red, blue, and yellow. They feed on maple, cherry, and birch leaves.
aldo.size: About the size of an open paperback at the wings.
aldo.look: Huge moth with brown-gray wings, reddish-orange bands and edges, white crescent eyespot on each wing. Furry red-and-white striped body.
aldo.home: Deciduous forests, woodland edges, suburbs in the eastern US.

facts: Named for the Cyclops in the Greek myth. The huge purplish eyespots on the hindwings are the giveaway.
Wingspan up to six inches. Lives across most of the continent in deciduous woods.
Adults have no working mouth. They live a few days, mate, and die. The whole point is the next generation.
aldo.size: About the size of a small open hand at the wings.
aldo.look: Big tan moth with rosy-brown bands across the wings, transparent yellow window-spots on the forewings, and large purple-blue eyespots ringed in yellow on the hindwings.
aldo.home: Forests and forest edges across most of North America.

facts: Hovers at flowers, holding still in the air, taking nectar with a long tongue. From a distance you'd swear it was a hummingbird.
Olive green and burgundy on the back, white or yellow underneath. Wings clear in the middle, with reddish-brown borders.
Flies in daylight, especially in summer afternoons. Most moths don't.
aldo.size: About the size of a thumb, mostly wings.
aldo.look: Stocky hawkmoth with a fuzzy olive-green and burgundy body, mostly clear wings with reddish-brown borders, long tongue. Hovers at flowers.
aldo.home: Gardens, meadows, woodland edges in the eastern US.

facts: Looks like a twig. That's the entire defense. They sit very still until they don't.
Common walking stick is about three to four inches long. Females are bigger than males.
Eats leaves. Hangs in shrubs and small trees. Most people walk past dozens and notice none.
aldo.size: About the size of a small pencil.
aldo.look: Long thin stick-like insect with six long thin legs, very long antennae, small head, slender body in green or brown to match the twigs they sit on.
aldo.home: Deciduous forests and shrubby edges across the eastern US.

facts: Among the largest beetles in the country. Up to two and a half inches, including the horn.
Males have a long horn on the head and another curving down from the thorax. Females are hornless.
Larvae live in rotting logs for two or three years before becoming adults.
aldo.size: About the size of a small lemon, including the horn.
aldo.look: Big rhinoceros beetle. Adults have green or tan elytra with black markings. Males carry a long upper horn from the thorax and a shorter horn on the head.
aldo.home: Deciduous forests of the southeastern US, especially with rotting hardwood logs.

facts: Slow, hairy, ground-living spiders. Most live in burrows in dry country.
Mature males walk overland in the fall looking for females. That's the famous tarantula migration.
Bite is painful but not dangerous to people. The bigger trouble is the urticating hairs they kick off the abdomen — they irritate skin and eyes.
aldo.size: About the size of a saucer, with legs spread.
aldo.look: Large hairy ground spider, brown to black, often with reddish or buff hairs on the abdomen. Eight stout legs, strong fangs, two small eyes raised on a turret.
aldo.home: Deserts, grasslands, and rocky open ground in the southwestern US.

facts: Sometimes called the toe-biter. They bite. The bite is painful, though not dangerous.
Big oval insect, two inches or more, with raptorial front legs for grabbing tadpoles, fish, and other bugs.
Female lays her eggs on the male's back. He carries them around until they hatch.
aldo.size: About the size of a credit card.
aldo.look: Large flat oval brown insect with strong forelegs for grabbing prey, paddle-shaped hind legs for swimming, dark beak folded under the head, two short breathing tubes at the rear.
aldo.home: Ponds, slow streams, marshes across the country. Sometimes flies to lights at night.

facts: Iridescent blue-black hindwings. The blue catches the light when the wings open.
Caterpillars eat plants in the genus Aristolochia — the pipevines. The toxins make them poisonous as adults.
Several other butterflies copy the look — the dark female tiger swallowtail, the spicebush swallowtail, and others — to share the protection.
aldo.size: About the size of a postcard at the wings.
aldo.look: Black butterfly with iridescent blue or green hindwings, single row of pale spots on the underside hindwing edges, dark forewings.
aldo.home: Forests, gardens, woodland edges where pipevines grow. Eastern US and parts of the Southwest.

facts: Bright yellow forewings on the male, reddish-brown on the female. Hidden under each forewing is a big black-and-blue eyespot — meant to startle.
When something gets too close, the moth flicks the forewings forward and shows the eyes. Birds usually leave.
Caterpillars are bright green with red and white side stripes — and stinging spines. Don't pick them up.
aldo.size: About the size of a credit card at the wings.
aldo.look: Medium silk moth. Male: yellow forewings. Female: reddish-brown forewings. Hindwings on both sport a big black-and-blue eyespot ringed in white.
aldo.home: Forests, edges, and yards in the eastern half of the country.

facts: The caterpillar is called the hickory horned devil. Five inches long, bright green, with red horns. Looks alarming. Doesn't sting.
Adult moth has gray-orange wings with yellow spots and orange veining. Wingspan up to six inches.
Eats hickory and walnut leaves as a caterpillar. Adults don't eat at all.
aldo.size: About the size of an open paperback at the wings.
aldo.look: Big silk moth with gray-tan forewings veined and edged in orange and yellow, large yellow spots, broad rusty hindwings. Furry orange-and-cream body.
aldo.home: Forests of the eastern half of the country, especially with hickory and walnut.

facts: Bright blue patches on the belly and throat. Sometimes called the blue-belly.
Does pushups on rocks and fence rails. Males do them to show off territory.
Common all over the West. On almost any sun-warmed rock, fence post, or trail, in summer.
aldo.size: About the size of a chalkboard eraser.
aldo.look: Small spiny lizard. Brown or gray on top with darker bars or blotches, long tail, blue belly and throat patches on males. Spiky scales along the back.
aldo.home: Rocks, fence rails, trails, sunny edges across the western US.

facts: Changes color, green to brown and back. Not for camouflage exactly — more about temperature and stress.
Sometimes called the American chameleon. Not a chameleon at all. Just changes color.
Males flash a pink throat fan, the dewlap, when claiming territory or impressing females.
aldo.size: About the size of a small carrot, including the tail.
aldo.look: Slim small lizard, usually bright green but sometimes brown. Long tail, big toe-pads for climbing. Pointed snout, alert eye. Males have a pink throat fan they flick out.
aldo.home: Trees, shrubs, fences, porches across the southeast.

facts: The call sounds like jug-o-rum, deep and slow. Carries across a pond at dusk.
Largest frog in North America. Some get to eight inches long.
Eats almost anything that fits in the mouth. Other frogs, snakes, mice, small birds.
aldo.size: About the size of a softball, hunched.
aldo.look: Large green-brown frog with darker mottling, white belly with yellow or gray spots, big round eardrum behind each eye, long powerful hind legs, fully webbed toes.
aldo.home: Ponds, lakes, marshes, slow streams. Anywhere with permanent water.

facts: An old box turtle is older than your grandfather. The only fact I'm sure of with these.
The shell hinges shut, top to bottom. They can close themselves entirely. That's the box.
Lives most of its life within a few hundred yards of where it hatched.
aldo.size: About the size of a small loaf of bread.
aldo.look: Small turtle with a high domed shell patterned in orange and yellow on dark brown, hinged plastron underneath, brown skin with yellow speckles. Males often have red eyes.
aldo.home: Forests, meadows, fields, sometimes yards across the eastern US.

facts: Red stripe behind each eye. That's the ear patch the name refers to. Easiest pond turtle to identify.
Native to the central and southern US, but now lives in ponds all over the world. People bought them as pets, and let them go.
Stacks up on logs to bask. Sometimes three or four turtles tall.
aldo.size: About the size of a dinner plate when full grown.
aldo.look: Medium pond turtle with a green-and-yellow striped head, bright red patch behind each eye, dark olive shell with yellow markings, webbed feet.
aldo.home: Ponds, lakes, slow rivers across the central and southern US, and naturalized almost everywhere with warm water.

facts: First frog of spring in the eastern woods. The chorus rolls out of every wet hollow on the first warm rain.
Tiny — about an inch long. Hard to find even when there are thousands singing all around you.
Dark X on the back. The species name crucifer means cross-bearer, for that mark.
aldo.size: About the size of a thumbtack.
aldo.look: Tiny chorus frog, tan or brown above with a darker X-shaped mark on the back, paler belly, sticky toe-pads for climbing. Big throat sac on calling males.
aldo.home: Wet woods, swamp edges, vernal pools. Eastern US.

facts: The call is a long musical trill. Males call from puddles and shallow water in spring.
Warty, brown to gray-brown, often with red or orange tints to the warts. The warts don't give people warts.
Lives almost anywhere that's damp at night and dry by day. Backyards, gardens, woodpiles, forest floors.
aldo.size: About the size of a small lemon, hunched.
aldo.look: Stocky brown or gray-brown toad with bumpy warty skin, large kidney-shaped paratoid glands behind the eyes, paler belly, short legs.
aldo.home: Yards, gardens, woods, fields. Anywhere damp at night across the eastern US.

facts: Bright apple green. Most have a clean white stripe down each side.
Sticks to walls and windows with toe pads. Not unusual to find one on the porch light at night.
Calls in chorus from ponds and ditches. The note is a nasal honk, repeated.
aldo.size: About the size of a half-dollar.
aldo.look: Slim bright-green tree frog with a smooth back, white or pale yellow stripe along each side from jaw to belly, big sticky toe pads, dark eye.
aldo.home: Wetlands, swamps, ditches, and trees near water in the southeastern US.

facts: Most common and widely distributed snake in North America. Found in all forty-eight contiguous states.
Three yellow stripes down a black, brown, or olive body. Sometimes red flecks between the stripes.
Harmless to people. Mildly venomous to small frogs and worms, but the bite doesn't matter to us.
aldo.size: About the size of a yardstick.
aldo.look: Slender snake, dark olive to black background with three yellow or cream stripes — one down the back, one along each side. Often red or orange flecks between the stripes.
aldo.home: Edges, fields, suburbs, woods, ditches. Almost anywhere near water.

facts: Young skinks have bright blue tails. The blue fades as they grow.
Five pale stripes down the back. They blur together on bigger adults.
Tail breaks off if grabbed. The piece keeps wiggling. The skink runs.
aldo.size: About the size of a small carrot, with a tail.
aldo.look: Small smooth lizard. Juvenile: black with five cream-yellow stripes and a bright blue tail. Adult: brown with fading stripes; males have orange jaws in spring.
aldo.home: Forest floors, log piles, rocky places, yards across the eastern US.

facts: Big males get over thirteen feet long. The biggest reach close to fifteen.
Almost gone in the 1960s. Now common again across the southeastern wetlands.
When the mouth is closed, you can't see the lower teeth. That's how you tell an alligator from a crocodile.
aldo.size: About the size of a small car.
aldo.look: Large dark-gray to black armored reptile with a broad rounded snout, heavy tail, four short legs, and bony plates along the back and tail.
aldo.home: Swamps, lakes, slow rivers, marshes from North Carolina to eastern Texas.

facts: Most widespread native turtle in North America. From Canada down to Louisiana, Atlantic to Pacific.
Smooth dark shell with red and yellow markings around the edge.
Fossils show painted turtles existed fifteen million years ago.
aldo.size: About the size of a salad plate when full grown.
aldo.look: Small to medium pond turtle with a smooth flat dark olive shell edged in red, yellow stripes on the head and neck, red and yellow stripes on the legs, yellow underside.
aldo.home: Ponds, slow streams, marshes, lakes across most of the country.

facts: Largest snake in much of the eastern US. Can reach six feet, sometimes more.
Excellent climber. Spends a lot of time in trees, looking for bird nests and squirrels.
Nonvenomous. They constrict their prey. People often mistake them for cottonmouths and kill them. Most snakes you see are not venomous.
aldo.size: About the size of a long broom handle.
aldo.look: Long slender black snake with a faint pattern of darker blotches visible up close, white or cream chin and throat, lighter belly with dark checkering.
aldo.home: Forests, barns, fields, rocky slopes across the eastern US.

facts: Lives three lives. Hatches in water, becomes a bright orange land-newt called an eft for a few years, then turns greenish-olive and goes back to water as an adult.
The red eft is what most people see — bright orange, walking through damp leaves on a wet summer day.
The skin makes a toxin. That's why the eft is so brightly colored — a warning.
aldo.size: About the size of a small carrot when fully grown.
aldo.look: Small salamander with three life stages. Eft: bright orange-red with darker spots, on land. Adult: olive-green above with red spots, yellow belly, in water.
aldo.home: Forest floors (eft) and ponds, lakes, slow streams (adult) across the eastern US.

facts: Only venomous lizard native to the United States.
Slow. Heavy. The bite is the danger, not the speed. They chew the venom in.
Black-and-pink or black-and-orange beaded skin. Looks made.
aldo.size: About the size of a small cucumber, two feet long.
aldo.look: Heavy-bodied lizard with bead-like scales, black-and-orange or black-and-pink mottling, thick tail, blunt head, forked black tongue. Slow on the move.
aldo.home: Desert scrub, rocky slopes, washes in Arizona, New Mexico, southern Utah, and southern Nevada.

facts: Largest rattlesnake on Earth. Heaviest venomous snake in the Americas. Some grow to seven feet.
Diamond-shaped pattern down the back, dark with light borders around each diamond.
The rattle on the tail is segments of dried skin from old molts. Each shed adds a new piece. The sound is dry, fast, unmistakable.
aldo.size: About the size of a long broom handle, much heavier.
aldo.look: Large heavy-bodied rattlesnake. Brown or olive with dark diamonds bordered in cream down the back, dark stripes through the eye, blunt heavy head, segmented rattle on the tail tip.
aldo.home: Pine flatwoods, palmetto scrub, coastal hammocks of the southeastern coastal plain.

facts: Largest salamander in North America. Up to two feet long.
Lives only in clear cold mountain streams under flat rocks. Sensitive to silt. Disappearing where streams get muddy.
Wrinkly skin, flat head, tiny eyes. Looks ancient because it is.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm.
aldo.look: Large flat-bodied salamander with wrinkly loose folds of skin along the sides, broad flat head, tiny eyes, four short legs, paddle-shaped tail. Brown to gray-brown above, pale below.
aldo.home: Clear cold rocky streams in the Appalachians and the Ozarks.

facts: Spends ninety-five percent of its life in burrows. Comes out for food and water when conditions are right.
Can live a hundred years or more.
Drinks rain when it falls. The bladder holds water for the dry months.
aldo.size: About the size of a deflated football.
aldo.look: Medium-large land tortoise with a high domed brown-tan shell with concentric ridges on each scute, blunt head, stout pillar-like front legs with heavy claws.
aldo.home: Mojave Desert in southern California, southern Nevada, southwestern Utah, and western Arizona.

facts: Spiky horns on the head and back. Built like a small flat dragon.
Eats ants, mostly. They sit by ant trails and pick them off one at a time.
Some species shoot blood from the corners of the eyes when threatened. The blood tastes bad to coyotes and dogs. They back off, usually.
aldo.size: About the size of a hand, flattened.
aldo.look: Flat round-bodied lizard, sandy-brown to gray with darker blotches, crown of spiky horns at the back of the head, spines along the sides. Short tail, short legs.
aldo.home: Sandy deserts, shrub-steppe, open ground in the western and southwestern US.

facts: The only rattlesnake across most of the populous Northeast. Lives in rocky ridges and old woods.
Dark crossbands on a yellow, tan, or gray background. Sometimes nearly black, with the bands hard to see.
Slow to bite. Most encounters end with the snake curled up and the person walking past, no rattle, no bite.
aldo.size: About the size of a long broom handle, heavy.
aldo.look: Heavy-bodied rattlesnake with dark V-shaped crossbands on a yellow, tan, gray, or near-black background. Wide triangular head, vertical pupils, segmented rattle on the tail.
aldo.home: Rocky forested ridges, hardwood slopes, mountain pine country across the eastern US.

facts: The mouth opens wide. Wider than the body in some lights. They eat almost anything that fits.
Most popular freshwater game fish in the country. Tournaments, boats, lures by the wall.
Native to most of the eastern half of the country. Stocked everywhere else.
aldo.size: About the size of a loaf of bread on a good day.
aldo.look: Stout greenish fish with darker mottled stripe down the side, white belly, very large mouth that extends past the eye, two-part dorsal fin.
aldo.home: Lakes, ponds, slow rivers across the country. They like cover — weeds, stumps, docks.

facts: Sometimes called bream or sunny. The first fish a lot of kids catch off a dock.
Dark blue-black flap on the gill cover. That's where the name comes from.
Builds nests on sandy lake bottoms in late spring. Males circle the nest and chase off anything that comes near.
aldo.size: About the size of a pancake.
aldo.look: Round flat-sided sunfish with olive-green back, blue and orange belly, dark vertical bars on the sides, dark blue-black ear flap on the gill cover.
aldo.home: Ponds, lakes, slow streams across the country.

facts: Most numerous catfish in North America. State fish of five different states.
Whiskers — barbels — at the mouth. Eight of them. They're for tasting and feeling, not for catching.
Eats almost anything. Live fish, dead fish, insects, plants, dough balls. Catfish anglers know this.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm, sometimes longer.
aldo.look: Long-bodied scaleless fish, slate-blue to olive-gray on the back, paler below. Eight whisker-like barbels around the mouth, deeply forked tail, small dark spots on the sides of young fish.
aldo.home: Rivers, lakes, ponds, reservoirs across the country.

facts: Native to Pacific Coast streams. Stocked all over the country now.
Pink to red stripe down the side, dark spots on the back and tail, pale belly.
When they go to sea and come back, they're called steelhead. Same fish, different life.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm in a stream, longer in big lakes.
aldo.look: Slender trout, olive to bluish-green back, silvery sides with a rosy-pink stripe, white belly, small black spots on body and tail. Pink stripe brightens during spawning.
aldo.home: Cold clear streams, mountain rivers, deep lakes across the country.

facts: Not a true trout. A char. Closer to lake trout and Arctic char than to rainbows.
Worm-like markings on the back — pale wavy lines on a dark green background. The pattern is unique to brook trout.
Lives in cold mountain streams. The cleaner and colder the water, the better.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm at most, often smaller.
aldo.look: Small trout with a dark olive-green back marked with pale wavy lines, red and yellow spots on the sides (red ones often haloed in blue), orange belly, white-edged orange fins.
aldo.home: Cold high-elevation streams in the eastern US, native. Stocked widely in the West.

facts: Bronze rather than green. The mouth doesn't reach past the eye, which is the easiest way to tell them from largemouth.
Lives in cooler, clearer water than largemouth. Rocky rivers and clean lakes mostly.
Red eye. Vertical bars on the sides instead of a horizontal stripe.
aldo.size: About the size of a loaf of bread on a good day.
aldo.look: Stout bronze-and-green fish with vertical dark bars on the sides, red-orange eye, two-part dorsal fin. Mouth ends below the eye, not past it.
aldo.home: Clear rocky rivers and lakes across the eastern and central US.

facts: Not native to the Americas. Brought from Europe in the 1800s. They've been here long enough now to feel at home.
Brown back, pale sides with red and black spots, often haloed in pale rings.
More wary than rainbows. Big browns are the hardest fish in many streams.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm in a stream, much bigger in lakes.
aldo.look: Long-bodied trout, brown to olive on the back, pale buttery-yellow sides with scattered black and red spots ringed in pale halos, white belly.
aldo.home: Cold streams and rivers across the country.

facts: Two species — black crappie and white crappie. Both speckled, both pan-shaped, both eaten from frying pans across the country.
The mouth tears easily on the hook. People call them paper-mouth.
Schools up around brush piles and submerged trees in spring. Move shallow to spawn, then deep again for summer.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dinner plate.
aldo.look: Round flat-sided panfish, silver to greenish, with dark speckles or vertical bars depending on species. Tall body, big eye, large mouth for the size.
aldo.home: Lakes, ponds, sloughs, slow rivers across the eastern and central US.

facts: Originally from Europe and Asia. Brought to the US in the 1800s on purpose. Now in lakes everywhere.
Big golden-bronze fish with two pairs of barbels at the mouth. Some get over forty pounds.
Stirs up the bottom feeding. Some lakes look muddy because of carp.
aldo.size: About the size of a small loaf of bread, sometimes much bigger.
aldo.look: Heavy-bodied fish with large gold-and-bronze scales, paler belly, two pairs of fleshy barbels at the corners of the mouth, long dorsal fin with a serrated leading spine.
aldo.home: Lakes, ponds, slow rivers across the country.

facts: Eyes look glassy in the dark. A reflective layer at the back of the eye lets them hunt in low light.
Sharp teeth. The mouth is full of them.
Native to most of Canada and the northern US. Especially common in Minnesota, Wisconsin, the Great Lakes.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm, sometimes much longer.
aldo.look: Long olive-gold fish with darker back, paler sides, two dorsal fins (the front one with sharp spines), white-tipped lower tail lobe, big glassy yellow eyes, sharp teeth.
aldo.home: Cool lakes and rivers across the northern and central US.

facts: Yellow with six or seven dark vertical bars across the sides. Easy to identify, easy to eat.
Closely related to the European perch — sometimes considered a subspecies, sometimes its own.
Schools by the thousands in lakes and ponds. Often the first fish kids catch through the ice.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dinner plate.
aldo.look: Slender fish with golden-yellow sides, six or seven dark vertical bars, white belly, two dorsal fins (the front one spiny), bright orange-red lower fins on adult males.
aldo.home: Lakes and ponds across the northern and central US.

facts: Largest of the Pacific salmon. Some over a hundred pounds.
Sometimes called king salmon. Spawns in fresh water, lives most of life in the ocean.
Coloration changes when they enter freshwater to spawn — silver-blue at sea, dull and reddish in the river, then dying after they spawn.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog.
aldo.look: Large salmon. At sea: dark blue-green back, silvery sides, small black spots on back and tail, black gums in the mouth. In rivers: dusky brown to red, hooked jaw on males.
aldo.home: Pacific Coast rivers (spawning) and the open ocean. Introduced to the Great Lakes.

facts: Long thin body, broad flat head, mouth full of teeth. Built like a torpedo with jaws.
Sometimes called jackfish or just northern. Common across the northern half of the country.
Pale spots on a dark green-brown background. The pattern is the same on every pike, but the size of the spots varies.
aldo.size: About the size of a yardstick, sometimes longer.
aldo.look: Long slender fish with a duckbill snout, big mouth full of sharp teeth, dark olive-green body with rows of pale yellow-cream spots, dorsal and tail fins set far back.
aldo.home: Weedy lakes and slow rivers across the northern US.

facts: Anadromous — lives in the ocean, spawns in fresh water. Some landlocked populations stay in lakes year-round.
Also called striper, rockfish, or linesider. Same fish, different coast.
Long, silvery, with seven or eight dark horizontal stripes down the sides.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm, sometimes much bigger.
aldo.look: Long streamlined fish, silvery white below and on the sides, blue-gray to dark olive on the back, with seven to eight dark horizontal stripes from the gill cover to the tail.
aldo.home: Atlantic coastal waters and rivers, also stocked in lakes and reservoirs across the country.

facts: Big black spot near the base of the tail. Sometimes more than one. Sometimes they have a whole row.
Also called channel bass or just red. Common from Massachusetts down to Mexico along the coast.
Sound carries underwater. Drum make a drumming sound with muscles against the swim bladder. The redfish drum at spawning time.
aldo.size: About the size of a forearm, sometimes much bigger.
aldo.look: Long bronze-red fish with a coppery sheen, lighter belly, one or more dark spots near the base of the tail, slightly underslung mouth.
aldo.home: Coastal waters, estuaries, bays of the Gulf and Atlantic coasts.

facts: Same species as the rainbow trout. The difference is the steelhead goes to sea and comes back.
Chrome-silver coming in from the ocean. They lose the silver and color up like a rainbow once they're in fresh water for a while.
Comes back to spawn in winter and spring. Big runs in the Pacific Northwest. The Great Lakes have stocked steelhead too.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog when they come in from the ocean.
aldo.look: Large rainbow trout, silvery on the sides and belly with a dark blue-green back, scattered small black spots, faint pink stripe down the side that brightens in fresh water.
aldo.home: Pacific Northwest rivers (spawning) and the open Pacific. Also stocked Great Lakes tributaries.

facts: Looks ancient because it is. The sturgeon body plan hasn't changed much in a hundred and fifty million years.
Bony plates instead of scales. A flexible cartilaginous skeleton instead of bone.
Lives a long time. Over a hundred years for some. The biggest are well over six feet.
aldo.size: About the size of a child, full grown, sometimes longer.
aldo.look: Big elongated fish with rows of bony plates along the back and sides, four whisker-like barbels in front of the toothless mouth, shark-like tail, slate-gray to olive-brown body.
aldo.home: Large rivers and lakes of the Great Lakes basin and the Mississippi drainage.

facts: The snout is half the body. Long flat paddle full of sensors that detect tiny prey in the water.
Filter-feeder. Swims with the mouth open, takes in water, filters out plankton through gill rakers.
Native to the Mississippi basin. Older than dinosaurs as a body plan.
aldo.size: About the size of a child, full grown.
aldo.look: Long fish with a paddle-shaped snout that takes up about a third of the body, smooth scaleless skin, gray on top, white below, deeply forked tail, large gill cover flap.
aldo.home: Large rivers and reservoirs of the Mississippi River basin.

facts: The species name versicolor means many colors. Brown, tan, gray, blue, sometimes orange — concentric rings on every shelf.
Grows on dead hardwood logs. A common decomposer in eastern woods.
Often appears in big stacked groups. Look like the fanned tails of small birds, hence the name.
aldo.size: About the size of a small clamshell at each cap.
aldo.look: Thin shelf-like polypore growing in clusters, fan-shaped, with concentric bands of brown, tan, gray, blue, and cream. White-pored underside.
aldo.home: Dead hardwood logs and stumps in forests across the country.

facts: The cartoon mushroom. Red cap, white spots. Real, and toxic. Don't eat one because it looks familiar.
Forms partnerships with the roots of pines, birches, spruces. Trades nutrients underground.
Spreads with planted pines. Now found around the world wherever northern conifers have been introduced.
aldo.size: About the size of a coffee mug at the cap.
aldo.look: Stout mushroom with a bright red or red-orange cap covered in white wart-like patches, white gills, white stem with a ring and a bulbous base ringed with small scales.
aldo.home: Conifer and birch forests across the northern and western US.

facts: Bright orange and yellow shelves on living and dead hardwoods. Visible from a distance through the trees.
Edible when young and tender. Texture similar to chicken meat — that's the name.
Comes back to the same trees year after year. The fungus lives inside the wood; the shelves are just the fruiting body.
aldo.size: About the size of a dinner plate at each shelf, often in stacks.
aldo.look: Bright orange or sulphur-yellow stacked polypore shelves with fan-like edges, soft fleshy texture when young, drying to white and brittle.
aldo.home: Hardwood trees, living or dead, across the country.

facts: Cultivated all over the world for food. First grown in Germany in World War I.
Shelf-like cap, off-center stem, gills running down the stem. Pale gray to white to tan, depending on age.
Decomposes wood. They break down even tough hardwoods into soil, given time.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dinner plate at each cap, often in clusters.
aldo.look: Pale gray, brown, or cream shelf-like mushroom with smooth caps, gills running down a short off-center stem, growing in overlapping clusters.
aldo.home: Dead hardwood logs and standing dead trees across the country.

facts: Honeycomb cap, hollow stem. Cut one open in half and you'll know it's a morel.
Comes up in spring, often around dead and dying elms, ashes, and apple trees. Sometimes on burned ground a year or two after a fire.
Highly prized by foragers. People keep their best spots secret for life.
aldo.size: About the size of a thumb at each mushroom.
aldo.look: Conical to round honeycomb-pitted cap, tan to dark brown, hollow inside, attached to a hollow whitish stem. Looks like a small honeycomb on a stalk.
aldo.home: Forests, riparian woods, and burned areas in spring across the country.

facts: Golden to yellow-orange, funnel-shaped. False gills on the underside — blunt ridges, not sharp blades.
Smells faintly fruity, sometimes like apricot. That's part of how foragers identify them.
Forms partnerships with oak, pine, and other forest trees. Trade goes both ways underground.
aldo.size: About the size of a small wineglass at each cap.
aldo.look: Funnel-shaped golden-yellow mushroom with wavy cap edges, false gills (forked blunt ridges) running down a tapering stem, fruity apricot scent.
aldo.home: Forests with oak, pine, and conifers, often on mossy ground. Across the country, especially Pacific Northwest and East.

facts: Massive white ball in a meadow. Sometimes basketball-sized. Sometimes bigger.
When mature, the inside turns to brown spore dust. A puff sends out billions of spores at once.
Edible when the inside is still pure white. Once it yellows, it's done.
aldo.size: About the size of a soccer ball, sometimes bigger.
aldo.look: Large white ball-shaped mushroom with smooth or slightly cracked skin, no visible stem, growing alone or in scattered groups. Inside white and firm when young, brown and powdery at maturity.
aldo.home: Meadows, fields, lawns, deciduous forest edges across the eastern and central US.

facts: White cascading spines hanging from a single soft mass. Looks like a frozen waterfall on a tree trunk.
Edible. Texture similar to crab or lobster when cooked.
Grows on dead and dying hardwoods, especially beeches and oaks.
aldo.size: About the size of a softball, sometimes much bigger.
aldo.look: White round mushroom hanging in a single clump from a tree, covered in long soft pendulous spines instead of gills. Yellows and browns with age.
aldo.home: Dead and dying hardwood trees in the eastern US.

facts: Shiny red-brown cap, shaped like a kidney or a fan. Almost looks varnished.
Grows on hardwood stumps and roots. Often goes unnoticed because it blends with the wood.
Used in Asian medicine for thousands of years. The name means spirit mushroom.
aldo.size: About the size of a small saucer at each cap.
aldo.look: Polypore mushroom with a glossy varnished red-brown to mahogany cap, paler edges, white pore surface underneath, often a thick lateral stem (or none).
aldo.home: Hardwood stumps and roots across the country.

facts: Pure white from cap to stem. Looks elegant, even harmless. Among the deadliest mushrooms in North America.
Eating one can be fatal. There's no antidote. Symptoms appear hours after eating, when the damage is already done.
Common in eastern oak and pine woods, summer through fall.
aldo.size: About the size of a coffee mug at the cap.
aldo.look: Slim all-white mushroom with a smooth dome-to-flat cap, white free gills, white stem with a hanging ring and a sac-like cup at the base.
aldo.home: Mixed deciduous and coniferous forests in the eastern US.

facts: Grows in a single huge cluster of gray ruffled fronds at the base of an oak.
Sometimes called maitake — Japanese for dancing mushroom. People who find a big one feel like dancing, the saying goes.
Comes back to the same tree year after year. A find worth remembering.
aldo.size: About the size of a small dog at the cluster.
aldo.look: Big cluster of overlapping gray-brown ruffled fan-shaped caps, each cap with a paler underside of small pores, all joined to a thick branching stem at the base.
aldo.home: Base of mature oak trees, sometimes other hardwoods, in the eastern US.

facts: Bright orange. Glowing gills, faintly, in the dark. A real bioluminescent mushroom, although the glow is weak — you need to dark-adapt.
Looks like a chanterelle to people who don't know better. Toxic. Causes serious gut upset.
Grows in dense clusters at the base of dead hardwoods.
aldo.size: About the size of a small saucer at each cap.
aldo.look: Bright orange mushroom with smooth funnel-shaped cap, true sharp gills running down the stem, growing in dense clusters at tree bases. Gills glow faintly green in the dark.
aldo.home: Base of dead hardwoods, especially oaks, in the eastern US.

facts: Brown cap on a thick white stem. A pore surface underneath, not gills. The stem has fine raised lines like a net.
Among the most prized edible mushrooms in the world. Italian markets dry and sell them all year.
Pacific Northwest and the Northeast both have good seasons for them. Especially under spruce and pine.
aldo.size: About the size of a coffee mug at the cap, with a fat stem.
aldo.look: Stout mushroom with a smooth brown cap, off-white to yellowish pore surface underneath (not gills), thick white-tan stem patterned with a faint raised network.
aldo.home: Conifer and mixed hardwood forests across the country, especially the West.

facts: Young caps ooze red liquid that looks like drops of blood. The drops dry into dark spots.
Spines under the cap instead of gills or pores — that's the tooth part.
Northern conifer forests, especially with old pines and spruces. Looks like nothing else in the woods.
aldo.size: About the size of a small biscuit at the cap.
aldo.look: Small white-to-pink toothed mushroom with a velvety cap exuding red liquid drops when young, drying to a darker patterned cap. Spines under the cap, short stocky stem.
aldo.home: Conifer forests in the northern and western US, especially old growth.

facts: All blue. Cap, gills, even the milk it bleeds when you cut it. Indigo, not painted on.
Edible. Holds the blue color when cooked, mostly.
Forms partnerships with oak and pine roots. Common in the eastern US in summer and fall after rain.
aldo.size: About the size of a coffee mug at the cap.
aldo.look: Blue to indigo mushroom with a slightly funnel-shaped cap (often with concentric darker rings), blue gills, blue stem. Bleeds blue milk when cut.
aldo.home: Oak and pine forests in the eastern and central US, also Asia and parts of Mexico.
